name: Flaw Pattern Practice Set
source: Original LR questions written for LSAT Trainer, five per flaw pattern at difficulty 2–5, in the style of PrepTests 150–159. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Term Shift, False Choice, Circular, Straw Man

questions.stimulus: League commissioner: Some fans complain that the Northfield Hockey League is no longer competitive, pointing out that the same two clubs have met in the championship final in each of the past five seasons. These fans are wrong. Our clubs now compete harder than ever for the region's best young players, offering contracts and training facilities far beyond anything they offered a decade ago. So the league is more competitive today than it has ever been.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the commissioner's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: dismisses the fans' complaint by questioning their motives rather than by addressing the evidence they cite
infers that the league's games are closely contested from the fact that clubs compete hard to sign players
presumes that what is true of the league's two most successful clubs is true of every club in the league
takes for granted that the clubs offering the largest contracts are the clubs that reached the championship final
treats the fact that the fans have not proven their claim as sufficient reason to reject that claim
questions.explanation: Equivocation: the fans use 'competitive' to mean that the games and standings are closely contested, while the commissioner's evidence shows only that clubs compete hard to sign players. (B) describes the bad inference from one kind of competition to the other. The tempting trap is (C), but the argument never moves from a trait of the top two clubs to the whole league.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The league is more competitive than ever, so the fans' complaint is wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Clubs now compete harder than ever to sign the best young players, with bigger contracts and better facilities.

breakdown.analysis: So what if clubs fight harder over recruits? The fans weren't talking about recruiting. They said the league isn't competitive because the same two clubs reach the final every year: the games and standings are lopsided. The commissioner answers with a different kind of competition: clubs competing in the market for players. Same word, two meanings. It's like saying a spelling bee is 'competitive' because schools compete to host it, when the complaint was that the same kid wins every year. Prephrase: the argument shifts the meaning of 'competitive.' This is equivocation. It's a classic; know it.

choices.note: The commissioner never attacks the fans' motives. He answers them, just with the wrong kind of evidence. This describes ad hominem, which isn't here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The fans say the league isn't competitive, but they're mostly supporters of losing clubs, so we can ignore them.

choices.note: CORRECT. The fans' claim is about how closely contested the games and standings are. The commissioner infers that the league is more competitive from evidence that clubs compete to sign players. That's a different kind of competition, so the inference rides on two meanings of one word.

Tempting, because the two finalist clubs are mentioned. But the argument draws no conclusion about every club from the top two. Its evidence is about all clubs' recruiting; the problem is what kind of competition that evidence shows.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our two best clubs have excellent coaches, so every club in the league has excellent coaches.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need this and doesn't assume it. Which clubs pay the most has nothing to do with the commissioner's reasoning.
The commissioner cites positive evidence (bigger contracts, better facilities); he doesn't rely on the fans' failure to prove anything. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the league is uncompetitive, so it must be competitive.

questions.stimulus: Wheat farmers in the arid Pellan Basin lose much of their harvest whenever rainfall is low. The new wheat variety Tamsk-4 has just been certified as drought-tolerant by the national seed board after three years of field trials. Therefore, Pellan Basin farmers who switch to Tamsk-4 can expect to harvest considerably more wheat in dry years than they now do.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: In years of normal rainfall, Tamsk-4 yields about as much grain per acre as the varieties now grown in the basin.
Some farmers in the Pellan Basin already irrigate part of their wheat fields during years of low rainfall.
Tamsk-4 seed costs somewhat more per acre than the seed that most Pellan Basin farmers currently plant.
The seed board certifies a variety as drought-tolerant if its plants survive prolonged drought, however little grain they produce.
Several wheat varieties that the seed board certified as drought-tolerant in past decades are no longer widely planted in the basin.
questions.explanation: The argument slides from 'drought-tolerant' in the seed board's sense to 'produces a good harvest in drought.' (D) shows the board's term means only that the plants survive, so certification says nothing about yield, which is what the conclusion is about. (E) is tempting, but varieties can fall out of use for many reasons (price, taste, disease), so it does not show Tamsk-4 will fail to raise dry-year harvests.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Farmers who switch to Tamsk-4 will harvest considerably more wheat in dry years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pellan farmers lose much of their harvest in dry years; Tamsk-4 is certified 'drought-tolerant' by the seed board.

breakdown.analysis: What does 'drought-tolerant' actually mean here? The conclusion is about harvest: more grain in dry years. The evidence is a label. If the label means 'the plant stays alive,' a field of living but nearly empty wheat plants would qualify. Prephrase: we want something showing the certification isn't about grain yield. It's like buying a 'waterproof' watch to go diving when 'waterproof' on the box only means it survives rain. Watch for weakeners that attack the meaning of a key term rather than the conclusion head-on.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument is about dry years. Matching yields in normal years says nothing about drought performance.
So? Some farmers irrigating part of their fields doesn't tell us whether Tamsk-4 will raise dry-year harvests. If anything, the rest still need help.
Wrong dimension. The conclusion is about how much wheat farmers will harvest, not whether switching is worth the money.
CORRECT. The board's 'drought-tolerant' means the plants survive, not that they produce grain. The conclusion needs the second meaning, so the certification no longer supports it.
Tempting, because it hints that certification hasn't worked before. But varieties drop out of use for lots of reasons: cost, disease, taste, a newer variety. Merely possible isn't enough to weaken.

questions.stimulus: The county's preservation ordinance requires that any building listed as historic by the county be preserved. The old Delmore grain elevator is unquestionably historic: it was the site of the 1931 farmers' strike, one of the most important events in the county's past. Therefore, the Delmore grain elevator must be preserved.
questions.stem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The library's rules allow any registered member to borrow rare books. Mr. Kato is unquestionably a member of the library's community: he has volunteered there every week for years. Therefore, Mr. Kato is allowed to borrow rare books.

Every employee whom the company designates as essential must report to work during storms. Raj's supervisor has formally designated Raj as essential. Therefore, Raj must report to work during the coming storm.
Every ingredient in the stew that Mia brought to the county fair is certified organic by the state agriculture board. Therefore, Mia's stew is itself certified organic by the state agriculture board.

Any athlete named to the all-star team receives a bonus from the league. Dara led the league in scoring this season, and the top scorer is almost always named to the all-star team. Therefore, Dara will receive a bonus.

Every vehicle registered as commercial must pay the toll on the Harbor Street bridge. Ana's van paid the toll on that bridge this morning. Therefore, Ana's van must be registered with the state as commercial.
questions.explanation: The ordinance covers buildings officially 'listed as historic,' but the argument shows only that the elevator is historic in the everyday sense of historically important: one word, two senses. (A) does the same with 'member': the rule covers registered members, and the argument shows only that Kato is a member of the community. Most students pick (D), because it too never shows the official status the rule requires; but (D) reasons from 'almost always' to 'will,' a probability-to-certainty error, and never trades on two senses of one word.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Delmore grain elevator must be preserved.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ordinance protects buildings the county has listed as historic; the elevator is historic because an important event happened there.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A rule covers things that have official status X; this thing is X in the everyday sense; so the rule covers it.

breakdown.analysis: Is 'historic' in the ordinance the same thing as 'historic' in the second sentence? No. The ordinance means 'on the county's list.' The evidence shows only 'important to history.' The argument slides from one sense to the other. It's like saying you can park in the faculty lot because you're a member of the faculty's book club. Prephrase: a rule about an officially defined status, then evidence that something has that status only in the ordinary sense of the same word. Most students pick (D), because a rushed prephrase is just 'it never shows the official status,' and (D) never shows Dara made the team. But (D)'s gap is a probability ('almost always') treated as a certainty. There's no word doing double duty.

choices.note: CORRECT. The rule covers 'registered' members; the evidence shows Kato is a 'member' only in the sense of belonging to the library's community. Same word, two senses, same leap to the rule's consequence.
Valid. The rule covers designated employees and Raj was formally designated. The official status is actually shown, so there's no flaw to match.
A part-to-whole move: every ingredient is certified, so the whole stew is. A different flaw, and no word shifts meaning.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every brick in the wall is light, so the wall is light.

choices.note: Tempting, because it also skips the official status. But its gap is different: 'the top scorer is almost always named' is treated as 'Dara was named.' That's a likely outcome treated as certain. 'All-star team' means the same thing throughout.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Rain usually cancels the game, and it's raining, so the game is definitely canceled.

choices.note: Reverses the conditional: commercial → pays toll; paid toll, so commercial. Many non-commercial vehicles pay tolls. A real flaw, but not this one.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All surgeons wear scrubs. Lee wears scrubs. So Lee is a surgeon.

questions.stimulus: Nursing administrator: State regulations require that every hospital unit have, on each shift, at least one nurse who is certified in critical care. Critics charge that our cardiac unit violated this rule last month, since on several night shifts the only nurse present with critical-care training had allowed her certificate to lapse. But her training was every bit as thorough as that of any certified nurse. So the unit complied with the regulation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the administrator's argument?
choices: The nurse whose certificate had lapsed was the most experienced nurse working on any of the cardiac unit's night shifts last month.
The critics would not have objected to the cardiac unit's staffing on those particular night shifts if the nurse's certificate had been current.
No other unit in the hospital went through even a single shift last month without a nurse who was certified in critical care.
Nurses whose critical-care certificates have lapsed are generally just as capable of caring for critically ill patients as nurses whose certificates are current.
A unit can comply with the regulation on a shift even if no nurse working that shift holds a current critical-care certificate.
questions.explanation: The rule requires a nurse 'certified' in critical care; the administrator shows only that the nurse was trained as thoroughly as a certified nurse. The argument works only if the rule's 'certified' can be satisfied without a current certificate, which (E) states without naming the term. Most students pick (D), because it sounds like the administrator's point; it fails because the question is whether the unit complied with the rule, not how well lapsed nurses care for patients in general, and negating (D) leaves this nurse's own training and the compliance question untouched.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cardiac unit complied with the regulation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule requires a nurse certified in critical care on each shift; on some night shifts the only trained nurse had a lapsed certificate; her training was as thorough as any certified nurse's.

breakdown.analysis: Does 'certified' mean 'holds a current certificate' or just 'trained to that level'? The critics read it the first way, and that's the natural reading. The administrator wins only if a shift with no currently certified nurse can still satisfy the rule. It's like claiming you drove legally because you drive as well as anyone with a license. Prephrase: the rule can be met without a current certificate. Notice the correct answer never says 'certified means trained.' It hides the point as a claim about compliance. Most students pick (D), because it echoes 'every bit as thorough.' But (D) is about patient care in general, not about what the rule requires.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument doesn't need her to be the most experienced; it needs her to satisfy the rule. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: The nurse whose certificate had lapsed was not the most experienced nurse working on any of the cardiac unit's night shifts last month.

choices.note: The critics' hypothetical reactions don't matter. Negate it and the compliance question is exactly where it was.
choices.negation: The critics would have objected to the cardiac unit's staffing on those particular night shifts even if the nurse's certificate had been current.

choices.note: Other units are out of scope. The conclusion is only about the cardiac unit.
choices.negation: Some other unit in the hospital went through at least one shift last month without a nurse who was certified in critical care.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like the administrator's whole case. But the conclusion is about compliance, not care quality, and about this nurse, not lapsed nurses 'generally.' Negate it: lapsed nurses generally aren't as capable. This nurse's training can still be thorough, and the rule question is untouched.
choices.negation: Nurses whose critical-care certificates have lapsed are generally not as capable of caring for critically ill patients as nurses whose certificates are current.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: a unit cannot comply on a shift if no nurse on that shift holds a current certificate. On those night shifts no one did, so the unit violated the rule and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: A unit cannot comply with the regulation on a shift if no nurse working that shift holds a current critical-care certificate.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Ridgeport Courier describes itself on its masthead as an independent newspaper, a term papers have long used to signal that they are not affiliated with any political party. Yet the Courier is owned by a corporation with large holdings in real estate and broadcasting, and a newspaper whose owner has such commercial interests cannot be independent of those interests. Thus, the Courier's description of itself is inaccurate.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the media critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that a corporation's commercial interests will shape what its newspaper chooses to report
attributes to the newspaper itself a characteristic that properly belongs only to the corporation that owns the newspaper
takes for granted that the newspaper claims to be independent in the sense in which the argument shows that it is not
attacks the newspaper's credibility by pointing to its owner's business interests rather than to the content of its reporting
concludes that the newspaper is affiliated with a political party merely because it is not free of commercial interests
questions.explanation: The Courier calls itself 'independent' in the sense of having no party affiliation; the critic shows it is not independent in another sense (free of commercial interests) and calls the self-description inaccurate. That works only if the Courier was claiming the second kind of independence, which (C) says, abstractly, the critic takes for granted. Most students pick (B), because the critic moves from the owner to the paper; but the critic gives an explicit premise for that move, and the real problem is that the claim the paper actually made could still be true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Courier's description of itself as independent is inaccurate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 'Independent' on a masthead traditionally means no party affiliation; the Courier's owner has big commercial interests; a paper with such an owner can't be independent of those interests.

breakdown.analysis: Independent of what? The masthead claim is 'not tied to a party.' The critic proves 'not free of commercial interests.' Both could be true at once: no party ties, plenty of business ties. So the critic refutes a claim the paper never made. It's like calling a 'sugar-free' label false because the candy has lots of calories. Prephrase: the critic assumes the paper meant the kind of independence the critic disproves. The correct answer says this without ever using the word 'independent.' Most students pick (B), because the argument does jump from the corporation to the paper. But the critic supplies a premise for that jump ('a newspaper whose owner has such interests cannot be independent of them'), so it isn't a bare part/whole slip.

choices.note: The critic doesn't need the owner's interests to shape what gets reported; the premise is only that the paper can't be independent of them. And even granting (A), the argument would still attack the wrong sense of 'independent.'

Tempting, because the argument moves from owner to paper. But that move comes with a stated premise, so nothing is attributed without a reason. The flaw is elsewhere: the paper's actual claim is about parties.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The parent company is huge, so each of its small subsidiaries is huge.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Independent' on the masthead means no party affiliation. The critic proves the paper isn't independent of commercial interests and treats that as refuting the masthead, which works only if the paper was claiming that second kind of independence.
The critic never questions the paper's credibility or reporting; the point is about whether a label is accurate. Not an attack on the source.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Don't believe the Courier's crime story; its owner sells real estate.

choices.note: The critic never says the paper is tied to a party. In fact the critic's argument ignores parties altogether, which is the problem.

questions.stimulus: Sales of the Brisa coffee maker have fallen for two straight years, while competing manufacturers have cut their prices on comparable models by nearly a third. So the Brisa's maker must either lower the Brisa's price to match its competitors' prices or stop producing it altogether. Since lowering the price that much would make the Brisa unprofitable, the company should discontinue it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the competitors' pricing decisions as evidence about the quality of the company's coffee maker
fails to establish that the coffee maker's sales have fallen faster than the sales of its competitors' comparable models
concludes that the coffee maker is already unprofitable merely because its sales have fallen for two straight years
presumes that what is true of the company's coffee maker is true of every product that the company makes
fails to consider that something other than a price cut could revive the coffee maker's falling sales
questions.explanation: False dichotomy: the argument treats 'cut the price' and 'discontinue' as the only options, ignoring others such as improving the product or advertising it differently. (E) says so. (C) is tempting, but the argument never says the Brisa is unprofitable now; the claim is that a deep price cut would make it unprofitable.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The company should discontinue the Brisa.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sales have fallen two years in a row; either cut the price to match competitors or discontinue; cutting the price would make it unprofitable.

breakdown.analysis: Why are those the only two choices? The company could redesign the Brisa, advertise it, add features, sell it in new stores, or just keep selling it at lower volume. The argument knocks out option one and declares option two the winner. That's a false choice. It's like saying: either I buy a new car or I walk to work; a new car is too expensive, so I'll walk. What about the bus? Prephrase: the argument ignores other options. This flaw (false dichotomy) is a classic; know it.

choices.note: The argument never treats competitors' prices as evidence of quality. It just mentions matching them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our competitors charge more, so their coffee makers must be better.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether competitors' sales also fell doesn't affect whether the two options are the only ones.
Tempting, but read carefully. The argument says lowering the price that much would make it unprofitable, not that it's unprofitable now. The argument doesn't draw this conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Sales fell, so we must be losing money on this product.

choices.note: The argument is only about the Brisa. Nothing is said about other products.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The Brisa is losing sales, so all our appliances are losing sales.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument treats a price cut and discontinuation as the only options. Other ways to revive sales (redesign, advertising, new stores) are never considered.

questions.stimulus: Last March the faint star Orvel-12 brightened tenfold for about two days and then returned to normal. A brightening like this can result from a flare on the star's surface or from gravitational lensing, which occurs when a massive object passes between us and the star. Flares change a star's color as it brightens, but Orvel-12's color stayed the same throughout. So the brightening was caused by lensing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: No process besides a flare or lensing is known to brighten a star tenfold without changing its color.
Some flares on stars similar to Orvel-12 have lasted considerably longer than two days before the star dimmed again.
Most of the stars that astronomers have seen brighten tenfold for a few days did so because of flares.
Flares on stars like Orvel-12 typically make the star appear redder rather than bluer while it is still brightening.
Lensing events involving stars as faint as Orvel-12 are only rarely detected, even by astronomers who search for them.
questions.explanation: The argument eliminates flares and concludes lensing, which works only if those are the only two possible causes; it treats 'can result from' as if it listed every possibility. (A) closes that gap by ruling out other known causes. (C) is tempting because it is about causes of brightening, but it actually makes flares more likely in general and so, if anything, weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lensing caused Orvel-12's brightening.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Such brightening can come from a flare or from lensing; flares change a star's color; Orvel-12's color didn't change.

breakdown.analysis: Are flares and lensing the only things that can do this? The argument says the brightening 'can result from' either, which isn't the same as 'can only result from' one of them. Knock out flares, and lensing wins only if there's no third suspect. It's like saying the cookies were eaten by the dog or the cat; the cat was locked out, so the dog did it. What about your little brother? Prephrase: we want an answer that rules out other causes. Strengtheners for a false-choice argument usually close the list of options.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument is a process of elimination with only two candidates. This answer confirms there's no known third candidate, so eliminating flares really does point to lensing.
Irrelevant. Flare duration doesn't matter; the argument eliminates flares by color, not by length.
Tempting, because it's about what causes brightening. But it says flares are the usual cause, which pushes against lensing. Wrong direction.
So? Which way flares shift the color doesn't matter. Orvel-12's color didn't change at all.
If anything this hurts: if lensing of faint stars is rarely seen, it's a less likely explanation. It doesn't help.

questions.stimulus: Sportswriter: The Fenwick Rovers' poor season was not the result of their star goalkeeper's departure, since the goalkeeper who replaced him posted statistics nearly identical to his. So the poor season must instead be the fault of the defensive system that the team's new coach introduced at the start of the season.
questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
choices: The Rovers began losing regularly within weeks of switching to their new coach's defensive system. So that system, and not the departure of the team's star goalkeeper, must be the cause of the Rovers' poor season.
Every ticket to the concert was bought either online or at the box office, and the box office sold no tickets at all for that concert. So every ticket to the concert must have been bought online.

The orchard's poor harvest was due either to the late frost or to the summer drought. Since the late frost clearly damaged the orchard's blossoms, the drought cannot have contributed at all to the poor harvest.

Higher flour costs are not what cut into the bakery's profits, since the bakery has paid the same flour price for over a year. So the drop in profits must be due to the new manager's staffing decisions.
The three Rovers fans interviewed by a local radio station after the final game all blamed the coach for the poor season. So most of the team's fans must blame the coach for the poor season.
questions.explanation: The sportswriter rules out one cause and blames the other, silently treating those two as the only possible causes: a false choice. (D) does exactly that with flour costs and staffing. Most students pick (A), because it has the same team, the same culprit and the same conclusion; but (A) blames the system because losses followed its adoption, a timing-to-cause flaw, and never eliminates a rival. (B) has the eliminate-one-option shape but states that the two options are exhaustive, so it is valid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new coach's defensive system is to blame for the poor season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The goalkeeper's departure wasn't the cause, since his replacement's statistics were nearly identical.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Not cause X; so cause Y (with X and Y silently treated as the only candidates).

breakdown.analysis: Why only those two suspects? Injuries, a tougher schedule, a weaker offense: none is ruled out. The sportswriter knocks out the goalkeeper and hands the blame to the coach as if nothing else could be responsible. It's like saying 'the butler didn't do it, so the gardener did.' Prephrase: an argument that eliminates one explanation and concludes a second, without ever saying those are the only two. Most students pick (A), because it's the same story with the same verdict. But (A) gets there by timing (losses began after the switch), not by elimination. Parallel flaw questions test the shape of the reasoning, not the topic.

choices.note: Tempting: same team, same culprit, same conclusion. But the reasoning is 'Y happened after X, so X caused Y.' Nothing is eliminated. That's a different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Sales fell right after we changed our logo, so the logo change caused the drop.

choices.note: The shape looks familiar (rule one option out, conclude the other), but here the premise says the two options are the only ones. With that stated, the conclusion follows. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.

Starts with 'either X or Y' and concludes that because X happened, Y played no part. That treats 'or' as 'only one.' A real flaw, but a different one: the original never confirms one cause to exclude the other.
choices.example: Example of flaw: You'll get in with good grades or good essays. Your grades are good, so your essay can't have helped.

choices.note: CORRECT. Flour costs are ruled out, so staffing must be to blame, with no reason given to think those are the only two possible causes. Same elimination step, same unstated two-option assumption.
A sampling flaw: three fans stand in for all fans. Nothing is eliminated here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The two diners I asked loved the soup, so most diners love it.

questions.stimulus: The Darrow Creek bridge can no longer safely carry loaded grain trucks. Repairing it would cost $4 million, while replacing it with a new bridge would cost $6 million. A repaired bridge would need major work again within fifteen years, but a new bridge would last at least fifty. Hence, the county should build a new bridge.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: A repaired Darrow Creek bridge would not remain safe for loaded grain trucks for more than ten years after the repairs.
Permanently closing the bridge to loaded grain trucks, while keeping it open to cars, would not serve the county better than a new bridge.
The county could pay for a new bridge without raising property taxes and without cutting funding for any of its other road projects.
Most of the vehicles that cross the Darrow Creek bridge on an ordinary weekday are loaded grain trucks bound for market.
A new bridge could be built in no more time than it would take to repair the existing bridge to a safe condition.
questions.explanation: The argument weighs only repair against replacement and concludes the county should replace; that requires that no option outside those two, such as closing the bridge to heavy trucks, would be better. (B) states that requirement for one specific alternative, which is why it looks irrelevant at first. Most students pick (C), because paying for the extra $2 million seems essential; but (C) is the right worry at the wrong strength: a bridge funded partly by a tax increase could still be the best choice, so (C)'s negation leaves the argument standing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county should build a new bridge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bridge can't safely carry loaded grain trucks; repair costs $4 million and lasts about fifteen years; replacement costs $6 million and lasts at least fifty.

breakdown.analysis: Repair or replace: are those really the only choices? The county could also keep loaded trucks off the bridge and leave it for lighter traffic, or route the trucks elsewhere. If one of those beats a new bridge, 'build a new bridge' is wrong. The argument picks the better of two options and calls it the best of all. It's like choosing between two expensive restaurants and concluding you should eat out, when cooking at home was never considered. Prephrase: some option other than repair or replacement isn't better. Most students pick (C), since cost feels central. But the argument only needs the bridge to be worth it, not to be paid for without any tax increase or any trade-off.

choices.note: Too strong and beside the point. The stimulus already says a repaired bridge needs major work within fifteen years; the argument doesn't need it to fail within ten. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: A repaired Darrow Creek bridge would remain safe for loaded grain trucks for more than ten years after the repairs.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: closing the bridge to loaded trucks while keeping it open to cars would serve the county better than a new bridge. Then the county shouldn't build a new bridge, and the conclusion fails. This is the overlooked third option, named specifically.
choices.negation: Permanently closing the bridge to loaded grain trucks, while keeping it open to cars, would serve the county better than a new bridge.

choices.note: Tempting, because someone has to pay the extra $2 million. But it's the right idea at the wrong strength: 'without raising taxes AND without cutting any other project.' Negate it: the county would need a tax increase or some cut. A new bridge can still be the right call.
choices.negation: The county could not pay for a new bridge without raising property taxes or cutting funding for at least one of its other road projects.

choices.note: Not needed. Even if most traffic is cars, the bridge still has to carry the grain trucks that do use it. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the vehicles that cross the Darrow Creek bridge on an ordinary weekday are loaded grain trucks bound for market.

choices.note: Not needed. A new bridge can take longer to build and still be the better investment over fifty years. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: A new bridge could not be built in as little time as it would take to repair the existing bridge to a safe condition.

questions.stimulus: Nurse manager: Critics claim that our hospital's practice of rotating nurses among units every six months harms patient care, since rotated nurses lose familiarity with each unit's routines. But in the two years since rotation began, rates of medication errors, patient falls, and readmissions on every unit have remained essentially what they were before. The critics are therefore mistaken, and rotation should be counted among the practices that improve the care our patients receive.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the nurse manager's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about a practice's long-term effects from data covering only the first two years after the practice began
confuses a correlation between a staffing practice and patient outcomes with a causal relationship between the two
overlooks the possibility that a practice can be free of a particular drawback without bringing about a corresponding benefit
presumes, without providing justification, that the critics' objection rests entirely on anecdotal reports from rotated nurses
fails to consider whether rotation has benefits or drawbacks for the nurses themselves, apart from its effects on patients
questions.explanation: Unchanged outcomes do undercut the critics' claim that rotation harms care, but the manager goes on to count rotation among practices that improve care, as if 'harms' and 'improves' were the only possibilities. (C) names the overlooked middle option, no effect at all, in abstract terms. Most students pick (A), because two years sounds like a short trial; but the conclusion is not about long-term effects, two years on every unit is not shown to be inadequate, and even with decades of flat data the leap from 'no harm' to 'improves' would remain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics are wrong, and rotation should be counted among practices that improve care.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In the two years since rotation began, error, fall and readmission rates on every unit stayed about the same.

breakdown.analysis: Flat numbers: what do they show? That rotation probably didn't make care worse. Fine. But 'improves care'? Nothing improved. The manager treats 'not harmful' as 'helpful,' skipping the obvious third option: rotation does nothing either way. It's like saying a new shampoo didn't make your hair fall out, so it must be making your hair healthier. Watch the jump from a polar opposite to a logical opposite: 'not harmful' isn't 'beneficial.' Prephrase: overlooks that the practice might have no effect. The right answer says it abstractly: free of a drawback without a benefit. Most students pick (A), because 'two years' invites a sample-size objection. But more data wouldn't fix the leap.

choices.note: Tempting, since two years can sound short. But the manager isn't concluding anything about the long term specifically, the data cover every unit, and nothing suggests problems would show up later. Even with ten years of flat numbers, 'no harm' still wouldn't mean 'improves.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: The new bridge stood fine through its first month, so it will last a century.

choices.note: There's no correlation to confuse: the outcomes didn't move. You can't infer cause from a change that never happened.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Test scores rose after the new cafeteria opened, so the cafeteria raised scores.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence supports 'rotation doesn't harm care.' The conclusion adds 'rotation improves care.' Between those sits the overlooked option: no harm and no benefit.
The manager says nothing about where the critics' view comes from; she answers it with data. No presumption about anecdotes.
Effects on the nurses are a different subject. The argument is about patient care, so ignoring nurse benefits isn't a flaw in it.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Diners choosing where to eat would do well to consult the Harlan Gazette first, because its restaurant reviews are the most reliable in the city. After all, our critics are the best judges of food in the city. And we know this because their reviews have proven more reliable than anyone else's.
questions.stem: The editor's argument is flawed because it
choices: treats the reliability of the Gazette's reviews as support for a claim offered to support that reliability
relies on the popularity of the Gazette's reviews among diners as evidence that those reviews are accurate
generalizes about all of the Gazette's reviews on the basis of only a few reviews by its critics
fails to specify what it would mean for one restaurant review to be more reliable than another
attacks the competence of rival critics instead of presenting evidence about the quality of the Gazette's own reviews
questions.explanation: Circular reasoning: the reviews are reliable because the critics are the best judges, and the critics are the best judges because their reviews are reliable. (A) describes this loop without naming it. (D) is tempting because 'reliable' is never defined, but an undefined term is not what makes the argument fail; even with a definition, the support would still run in a circle.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Diners should consult the Gazette first, because its restaurant reviews are the most reliable in the city.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its critics are the best judges of food; we know that because their reviews are the most reliable.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the outside evidence? Trace it: reviews are reliable ← critics are the best judges ← reviews are reliable. The conclusion shows up again as the support for its own premise. That's circular reasoning. It's like saying 'I'm trustworthy because I always tell the truth, and you know I tell the truth because I'm trustworthy.' Prephrase: the argument assumes what it's trying to prove.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Critics are the best judges' is offered to support the reviews' reliability, but its only support is that same reliability. The argument uses its conclusion to prop up its own premise.
Popularity isn't mentioned. The support is the critics' supposed judgment, not how many people read them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: More people read our reviews than any others, so they must be the most accurate.

choices.note: No sample of reviews is cited at all. That's part of the problem, but it's not a hasty generalization.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our last two reviews were spot on, so all our reviews are reliable.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'reliable' is vague. But defining it wouldn't fix anything: the support would still loop back to the conclusion. Pick the flaw the argument actually commits.
The editor never attacks rival critics. Nothing is said about anyone else's competence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The Tribune's reviewers are amateurs who can't cook, so our reviews are better.

questions.stimulus: Nurses at Linfield Hospital now use the Corbel Pain Scale, on which patients rate their pain by choosing among a series of drawn faces. This scale accurately measures patients' pain. After all, in a recent study on the hospital's surgical ward, patients' Corbel scores closely matched the pain levels that their nurses assigned them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Patients find the Corbel scale much easier to use than any of the pain scales that the hospital used previously.
Nurses' assessments of patients' pain are generally more accurate than patients' own descriptions of how much pain they feel.
Most of the patients in the study were experiencing at least moderate pain at the time when they were assessed.
The nurses in the study did not base their assessments of patients' pain on the patients' Corbel scores.
No other pain scale has been shown to match nurses' assessments of pain as closely as the Corbel scale does.
questions.explanation: The study validates the Corbel scale by checking it against nurses' assessments; if the nurses simply read off the Corbel scores, the match would be guaranteed and would prove nothing, making the support circular. (D) rules this out. (B) is tempting, but it is too strong: the argument needs nurses' assessments to be a reasonable, independent check, not better than patients' own reports.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Corbel scale accurately measures patients' pain.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a study, patients' Corbel scores closely matched the pain levels nurses assigned them.

breakdown.analysis: What if the nurses got their numbers from the Corbel scale? Then the scores would match because they're the same scores, and the 'test' would just check the scale against itself. A match only means something if the two measures are independent. It's like proving your bathroom scale is accurate by noting it agrees with what you wrote down from your bathroom scale. Prephrase: the nurses' ratings weren't derived from the Corbel scores. Necessary-assumption tip: negate each choice and see if the argument breaks.

choices.note: Ease of use is a different question from accuracy. Wrong dimension.
choices.negation: Patients do not find the Corbel scale much easier to use than every one of the pain scales that the hospital used previously.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs the nurses' ratings to be a decent independent check, not better than patients' own reports. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Nurses' assessments of patients' pain are not generally more accurate than patients' own descriptions of how much pain they feel.

choices.note: Not needed. A scale can match nurses' judgments across mild pain too. Negating this doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Most of the patients in the study were not experiencing at least moderate pain at the time when they were assessed.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the nurses based their ratings on the Corbel scores. Then the match is automatic and shows nothing about accuracy. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The nurses in the study based their assessments of patients' pain on the patients' Corbel scores.

choices.note: Not needed. The conclusion is that Corbel is accurate, not that it's the most accurate. Another scale doing as well wouldn't hurt.
choices.negation: Some other pain scale has been shown to match nurses' assessments as closely as the Corbel scale does.

questions.stimulus: Architect: The Merrow Library is the most successful public building in our city. The success of a public building should be judged by the opinions of people qualified to evaluate architecture. And anyone who fails to see the Merrow Library's superiority to the city's other public buildings plainly lacks such qualifications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the architect's argument?
choices: Dr. Imre's book is the best history of the region ever written. Every historian who has reviewed the book has praised it highly, and historians are clearly the people best qualified to judge works of history.

The Rialto is the best theater in town. A theater's quality should be judged by how many people choose to attend it, and more people attended performances at the Rialto last year than at any other theater in town.

Most critics of the Merrow Library's design are architects whose own proposals for the library were rejected by the city. So their criticisms are probably motivated by resentment and should not be taken seriously.

Anyone with a discerning palate appreciates Calla's cider, and Jo appreciates Calla's cider more than any other drink. So Jo must have a discerning palate, and her opinions about other ciders deserve our trust.

Anyone who does not prefer Calla's cider to the valley's other ciders obviously lacks a discerning palate, and cider should be judged by people who have one. So Calla's cider is the best cider made in the valley.
questions.explanation: The architect defines the qualified judges as exactly those who agree with the conclusion, so the appeal to their judgment presupposes what it is meant to prove. (E) does the same with 'discerning palate,' though it puts the definition first and the conclusion last. Most students pick (A), because it also rests a 'best' claim on the verdict of qualified judges; but historians are identified independently of whether they praise the book, so (A) is an ordinary appeal to authority, not a circle.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Merrow Library is the city's most successful public building.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Success should be judged by people qualified to evaluate architecture; anyone who doesn't see the library's superiority isn't qualified.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X is best; judge by qualified judges; anyone who doesn't think X is best isn't qualified.

breakdown.analysis: How do we know who's qualified? By whether they agree the library is best. So 'the qualified judges agree' is guaranteed: anyone who disagrees is thrown out of the jury. The conclusion is built into the definition of the judges. It's like a contest whose judges are 'everyone who votes for me.' Prephrase: an argument that appeals to judges and then defines the judges as the people who reach the desired verdict. Order doesn't matter in parallel questions; the right answer may put the conclusion last. Most students pick (A), because it's the closest-sounding appeal to qualified judges. But in (A) the judges qualify by being historians, whatever they think of the book.

choices.note: Tempting, since it also appeals to qualified judges. But historians are qualified for reasons that have nothing to do with liking this book. That's an ordinary (maybe weak) appeal to authority, not a circle.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every dentist I asked recommends this toothpaste, so it's the best toothpaste.

choices.note: An appeal to popularity, not circular reasoning. The standard (attendance) is set independently of the conclusion, and attendance figures are outside evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This song is the year's best because it was streamed the most.

choices.note: An attack on the critics' motives, using the same library to lure you. No circle.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ignore the senator's tax plan; she's rich.

choices.note: Same cider, different flaw: it reverses a conditional. Discerning → appreciates; Jo appreciates, so Jo is discerning. No one is defined into agreement.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All doctors know CPR. Sam knows CPR. So Sam is a doctor.

choices.note: CORRECT. Discerning judges are defined as those who prefer Calla's cider, and their verdict is then used to prove Calla's is best. Same circle as the architect's 'qualified' people, just written in a different order.

questions.stimulus: The unsigned 1872 editorial in the Corley Sentinel opposing the railroad tax was written by Rhoda Pell, the paper's editor at the time. The editorial contains several unusual turns of phrase, and each of these phrases also appears in at least one of the editorials attributed to Pell in the standard catalogue of her work. No other writer of that period is known to have used these phrases.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Pell was not the only writer working for the Sentinel in 1872 who publicly opposed the proposed railroad tax in print.
Some of the editorials that the standard catalogue attributes to Pell contain none of the unusual phrases found in the 1872 editorial.
The editorials that share those phrases were credited to Pell in the catalogue chiefly because the 1872 editorial, long presumed hers, contains them.
The Sentinel published unsigned editorials more often in 1872 than in any other year during which Pell edited the paper.
The standard catalogue of Pell's work was compiled more than fifty years after her death by a single scholar working alone.
questions.explanation: The argument treats the catalogue's attributions as independent evidence of Pell's style. (C) shows that the editorials sharing the phrases were assigned to her precisely because the 1872 editorial was presumed hers, so using them to prove that editorial is hers runs in a circle and the match is no evidence at all. Most students pick (E), because it casts doubt on the catalogue; but a late, single-author catalogue can still be accurate, and (E) says nothing about how these particular attributions were made.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pell wrote the unsigned 1872 editorial.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its unusual phrases each appear in editorials the standard catalogue attributes to Pell; no other writer of the period is known to have used them.

breakdown.analysis: Why does the catalogue say those other editorials are Pell's? If it's because they sound like the 1872 editorial, and the 1872 editorial was assumed to be hers, then the evidence loops back on itself: 1872 is hers because it matches her catalogue, and the catalogue is hers because it matches 1872. It's like confirming a rumor by checking with the people who heard it from you. Prephrase: show the attributions aren't independent of the conclusion. Most students pick (E), because it questions the catalogue's reliability. But 'late' and 'one scholar' don't show any attribution is wrong. (C) shows exactly why these attributions prove nothing.

choices.note: Other writers opposing the tax doesn't matter: the argument rests on the phrases, and no one else is known to have used them. Topic matches, evidence doesn't.
Expected, and harmless. Writers don't use their pet phrases in every piece. The argument only needs the phrases to show up in some Pell editorials.
CORRECT. The 'match' with Pell's catalogued work was manufactured by presuming the 1872 editorial was hers. So the argument uses its own conclusion as evidence, and the support disappears.
Interesting fact, but it doesn't touch the phrase evidence. More unsigned editorials in 1872 doesn't make this one less likely to be Pell's.

Tempting, since it attacks the catalogue. But it's only a vague worry about the source: a late, single-author catalogue can be perfectly accurate. It gives no reason to think these attributions are wrong, and it misses the circle.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Critics charge that the council acted improperly in approving the Fennell Road rezoning without first holding a public hearing. But the town charter requires a public hearing only for rezonings that substantially change the character of a neighborhood. And the Fennell Road rezoning made no such change, as is shown by the fact that the council, which always holds a hearing when the charter requires one, saw no need to hold a hearing on it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses a condition required for a hearing to be mandatory with a condition that guarantees a hearing is mandatory
takes for granted that the council's judgment was correct on the very point that the critics dispute
fails to consider that a rezoning might change a neighborhood's character in ways that fall short of being substantial
rejects the critics' charge on the grounds that the critics have not proven that the rezoning changed the neighborhood's character
draws a general conclusion about the council's conduct in all rezonings on the basis of a single decision
questions.explanation: The critics dispute the council's judgment that no hearing was needed, yet the council member's only evidence that the rezoning was not substantial (and so needed no hearing) is that the council saw no need for one. (B) identifies this circle. Most students pick (A), because the charter states an 'only' conditional and conditional confusions are a classic flaw; but the argument applies it correctly: a hearing is required only if the change is substantial, so a non-substantial change requires no hearing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council acted properly in approving the rezoning without a hearing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A hearing is required only if a rezoning substantially changes a neighborhood; this one didn't, because the council (which always holds required hearings) saw no need for one.

breakdown.analysis: How do we know the rezoning wasn't substantial? Because the council didn't hold a hearing. But whether the council was right to skip the hearing is exactly what the critics are challenging. The member answers 'Was the council right?' with 'Yes, because the council decided so.' The conditional part is fine: hearing required → substantial change. Contrapositive: no substantial change → no hearing required. That's valid. It's like a referee saying 'that wasn't a foul, because I'd have called it if it were.' Most students pick (A), because they see 'only' and reach for necessary-versus-sufficient. Diagram it before you accuse the argument of a conditional error.

choices.note: Tempting, because there's an 'only' conditional in the stimulus. But the argument handles it correctly: substantial change is necessary for a required hearing, so no substantial change means no required hearing. No confusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A hearing is required only for substantial changes. This change is substantial, so a hearing was required.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critics say the council wrongly skipped a hearing. The member's proof that skipping was right is that the council skipped it. That takes the disputed judgment as settled.
Irrelevant. Non-substantial changes don't trigger the charter, so overlooking them costs the argument nothing.
The member doesn't rely on the critics' lack of proof. He offers his own evidence (the council's judgment). That evidence is circular, but it isn't an absence-of-evidence argument.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics haven't proven the neighborhood changed, so it didn't.

choices.note: The member draws no general conclusion; he talks only about this rezoning. 'Always holds required hearings' is a premise, not a conclusion drawn from one case.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The council handled this rezoning well, so it handles every rezoning well.

questions.stimulus: Jolene Varga has proposed that the Tarrow Grain Cooperative require members to have their stored grain tested for mold before delivery after unusually wet harvests. But Varga apparently wants every load of grain sent to a laboratory year after year, no matter what the weather has been. A requirement like that would bankrupt the cooperative's smaller members, so her proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument
choices: fails to consider that laboratory testing for mold might cost far less than the cooperative's smaller members expect it to
presumes that whatever would harm the cooperative's smaller members would also harm every other member of the cooperative, large or small
rejects Varga's proposal on the basis of her character rather than on the basis of the merits of the proposal itself
presumes, without providing justification, that Varga wants every load of grain tested every year regardless of the weather
takes for granted that unusually wet harvests occur too rarely to justify any testing requirement
questions.explanation: Straw man: Varga proposed testing only after unusually wet harvests, but the argument, with no justification, recasts her proposal as testing every load every year and attacks that. (D) describes the unsupported recasting. (A) is tempting because cost drives the objection, but even if lab tests were expensive, the objection still targets a proposal Varga never made.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varga's proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Varga 'apparently' wants every load tested every year; that would bankrupt small members.

breakdown.analysis: Is that what Varga proposed? No. Her proposal is testing after unusually wet harvests. The argument swaps in a much bigger version (every load, every year, any weather) and knocks that down. That's a straw man. It's like someone suggesting you wear a coat when it snows, and you reply that wearing a coat every day of summer would be ridiculous. Prephrase: the argument attacks a distorted version of the proposal. Straw man is a classic; know it.

choices.note: Tempting, since cost is the stated objection. But the core problem isn't the price of a test. Even if testing were costly, the argument still attacks the wrong proposal.
The argument never says the requirement would harm every member, only that it would bankrupt the smaller ones. No part/whole move.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Small farms would suffer, so the whole co-op would suffer.

choices.note: Nothing is said about Varga's character. The argument attacks (a version of) the proposal, not the person.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Varga has never run a farm, so ignore her proposal.

choices.note: CORRECT. Varga proposed testing only after unusually wet harvests. The argument simply declares that she 'apparently' wants year-round testing of every load, offers no reason to think so, and then attacks that version.
The argument takes nothing for granted about how often wet harvests occur. If anything, it ignores the wet-harvest limit entirely.

questions.stimulus: The nurses' union at Halvern Hospital says that twelve-hour shifts cause fatigue-related errors, and it has proposed cutting back on their use. But eliminating twelve-hour shifts would leave the hospital's night units badly understaffed, since many nurses work nights only because a twelve-hour schedule lets them work three days a week. So the union's proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Many of the nurses who prefer twelve-hour shifts do so because they commute long distances to the hospital.
Fatigue-related errors are more common during the final hours of long shifts than during their first few hours.
Nurses who work on the hospital's night units are paid more per hour than nurses who work during the day.
Several other hospitals in the region have ended twelve-hour shifts within the past five years, citing nurses' fatigue.
The union proposes ending twelve-hour shifts only in intensive care, whose nurses do not staff the night units.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects the proposal because eliminating all twelve-hour shifts would understaff the night units, but (E) shows the union proposed something narrower that would not touch those night units, so the objection attacks a proposal the union didn't make. (B) is tempting because it supports the union's concern about fatigue, but it leaves the staffing objection untouched; (E) removes the basis of that objection.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The union's proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ending twelve-hour shifts would understaff night units, because many night nurses rely on the three-day schedule.

breakdown.analysis: Is the argument attacking what the union actually proposed? The union proposed to 'cut back on their use,' but the argument attacks eliminating twelve-hour shifts altogether. If the proposal is narrower and doesn't touch the night units, the understaffing objection misses entirely. Prephrase: show that the proposal wouldn't affect the night units' schedules. It's like objecting to a ban on phones in the exam room by saying people need phones to call home: the ban doesn't cover the hallway. A great weakener here exposes a straw man.

choices.note: This explains why some nurses like long shifts, which if anything supports the staffing concern. Wrong direction.
Tempting: it backs the union's fatigue worry. But the argument never denied fatigue; its reason is staffing. This leaves that reason standing, so it only slightly helps the union.
Irrelevant. Night pay rates don't affect whether ending twelve-hour shifts would understaff night units.
So? Other hospitals' choices don't show this hospital's night units would be fine.
CORRECT. The proposal covers only intensive care, whose nurses don't staff the night units. So the night units wouldn't be understaffed, and the objection targets a proposal that wasn't made.

questions.stimulus: Some reporters at the Dunmore Herald have suggested that the paper skip its Monday print edition during the summer months, when advertising is scarce. But a newspaper that abandons its print edition gives up its most loyal readers, many of whom do not use the Internet at all. So the reporters' suggestion would be a serious mistake.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Some members have suggested that the gym close on Sundays. But Sunday is the gym's busiest day of the week, so closing then would cost the gym more revenue than closing on any other day. So the members' suggestion would be unwise.

Some residents have suggested that the town close its pool on Tuesdays during the off-season. But a town that shuts down its pool leaves its children without a safe place to swim all summer. So the residents' suggestion should be rejected.

Some residents have suggested that the town close its public pool on Tuesdays. But if the pool closes on Tuesdays, it will soon close on Wednesdays as well, and eventually it will close for good. So the residents' suggestion should be rejected.

Some residents have suggested that the town either keep its public pool open every day or close it permanently. Keeping it open every day would be too costly. So the town should close the pool permanently.

Some lifeguards have suggested that the town close its public pool on Tuesdays. But those lifeguards would enjoy an extra day off if the pool closed, so their suggestion should not be taken seriously.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects a limited suggestion (skip Monday editions in summer) by citing the costs of a far more drastic one (abandoning print altogether), so it attacks a proposal no one made. (B) does the same, answering a plan to close one off-season day with the harms of shutting the pool down. Most students pick (C), because it also rejects a modest closing by pointing to a drastic one; but (C) predicts the modest step will lead to the drastic one, a slippery-slope argument, and never misdescribes what was proposed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reporters' suggestion would be a serious mistake.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A paper that abandons its print edition loses its most loyal readers.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Someone proposes a small, limited change; the arguer cites the harms of a much bigger change; so the proposal should be rejected.

breakdown.analysis: Did anyone suggest abandoning print? No: just skipping Mondays in the summer. The argument swaps in a bigger, scarier proposal and knocks that down. That's a straw man. It's like answering 'let's skip dessert tonight' with 'giving up food entirely would make you sick.' Prephrase: a limited proposal rejected because of the harms of a sweeping version nobody proposed. Most students pick (C), because it's the other answer where a small closing leads to talk of a permanent one. But (C) argues the small step will cause the big one. It doesn't pretend the proposal was the big one.

choices.note: A reasonable objection: it addresses the actual proposal (Sundays) and gives a relevant reason (lost revenue). Nothing is distorted.
CORRECT. The proposal is one off-season weekday; the objection is about shutting the pool down for the summer. Same switch from a limited proposal to a sweeping one.

Tempting, because a small closing gets tied to a permanent one. But this is a slippery slope: it predicts the small step will snowball. It responds to the real proposal, just with an unsupported prediction.
choices.example: Example of flaw: If we let students retake one quiz, soon they'll demand to retake every exam.

choices.note: A false choice: only two options are considered. The proposal isn't misdescribed.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Either we hire ten new teachers or we close the school. We can't afford ten, so we must close.

choices.note: Attacks the lifeguards' motives instead of their proposal. Ad hominem, not a straw man.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The union wants shorter shifts only because its members are lazy, so ignore the proposal.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Some consumer groups have urged the state to require that every household cleaning product list all of its chemical ingredients on its label. These groups evidently believe that ordinary shoppers can make sense of dozens of unfamiliar chemical names. But most shoppers cannot tell one chemical from another. So the groups' proposal rests on a false belief and should not be adopted.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the columnist's argument depends?
choices: Complete ingredient lists would not be worth requiring merely for the help they could give people other than ordinary shoppers.
Most shoppers do not read the labels that household cleaning products currently carry before deciding which product to buy.
The consumer groups have no evidence that any household cleaning product now on the market harms its users.
No shopper would be able to make sense of the chemical names that a complete ingredient label would list.
The members of the consumer groups are themselves able to make sense of the chemical names on product labels.
questions.explanation: The columnist pins one rationale on the groups (ordinary shoppers will understand the names), refutes it, and concludes the proposal should not be adopted. That conclusion requires that the proposal not be justified on some other ground, for example by helping doctors or poison-control staff who can read the names. (A) rules out that defense. Most students pick (D), because it restates the columnist's key premise; but it is the right idea at the wrong strength: the columnist says only that most shoppers can't tell chemicals apart, and if a few can, the argument is unharmed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The groups' labeling proposal rests on a false belief and should not be adopted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The groups evidently think ordinary shoppers can make sense of chemical names; most shoppers can't tell one chemical from another.

breakdown.analysis: Is shopper comprehension really the only reason to list ingredients? A full list could help a doctor treating a child who swallowed a cleaner, or a poison-control line. The columnist picks one rationale, the weakest, refutes it, and throws out the whole proposal. That's a straw-man move. It's like rejecting smoke detectors because most people can't repair the wiring. Prephrase: the proposal isn't justified by benefits to anyone other than shoppers who'd need to read the names. Notice the right answer looks irrelevant at first: it's about other people. Most students pick (D), because it sounds like the columnist's own point. But the columnist only claims 'most.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: complete lists would be worth requiring just for the help they give others, like doctors or poison-control staff. Then the proposal deserves adoption even if shoppers are baffled, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: Complete ingredient lists would be worth requiring merely for the help they could give people other than ordinary shoppers.

choices.note: If anything this would be another reason to doubt the proposal, but the argument doesn't need it. Negate it (most shoppers do read labels) and the columnist's reasoning about comprehension is unchanged.
choices.negation: Most shoppers do read the labels that household cleaning products currently carry before deciding which product to buy.

choices.note: Out of scope. The argument is about whether shoppers can understand the lists, not whether any product is harmful. Negating it adds a reason for labels but doesn't touch the columnist's chain.
choices.negation: The consumer groups have evidence that at least one household cleaning product now on the market harms its users.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the columnist's premise turned up to full volume. Too strong. The columnist says most shoppers can't tell chemicals apart. Negate it: some shopper could make sense of the names. The argument is fine.
choices.negation: At least one shopper would be able to make sense of the chemical names that a complete ingredient label would list.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the groups' own members can read chemical names says nothing about whether the proposal is justified.
choices.negation: The members of the consumer groups are not themselves able to make sense of the chemical names on product labels.

questions.stimulus:
Ostrova: The observatory should stop letting a single committee made up entirely of senior staff decide which proposals receive time on its main telescope. Committees drawn from a single group tend to favor the kinds of projects that group already knows.

Haddad: Ostrova is mistaken. Our senior staff are among the most accomplished astronomers in the world, and many of the observatory's best-known discoveries came from projects they selected. There is no reason to think that less accomplished astronomers would choose better projects.
questions.stem: Haddad's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes that astronomers who have made important discoveries are infallible judges of the proposals other astronomers submit
takes for granted that the observatory's best-known discoveries are also the most scientifically important of all the ones it has ever made
treats a concern about how narrowly a committee is drawn as a proposal to fill it with less capable judges
concludes that the committee's past choices have been sound merely because no one has yet shown that any of them were unsound
draws a conclusion about all of the observatory's staff from the accomplishments of only its most senior members
questions.explanation: Ostrova objects that a committee drawn entirely from one group is too narrow; she never proposes swapping in less accomplished astronomers, yet Haddad rebuts exactly that. (C) describes this misreading abstractly, without naming either speaker. Most students pick (A), because Haddad leans heavily on the staff's accomplishments; but it is the right idea at the wrong strength: Haddad claims only that others would not choose better, not that the senior staff never err.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Haddad: Ostrova is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The senior staff are accomplished and chose the projects behind famous discoveries; there's no reason to think less accomplished astronomers would choose better.

breakdown.analysis: Who said anything about less accomplished astronomers? Ostrova's complaint is about breadth: one group judging everything favors that group's kind of project. She could want a mixed committee with senior staff on it. Haddad answers a proposal to replace the experts with weaker judges, which nobody made. That's a straw man. It's like answering 'the hiring panel shouldn't be all engineers' with 'non-engineers don't know engineering.' Prephrase: Haddad misreads a complaint about makeup as a call for worse members. Most students pick (A), because Haddad does lean on the staff's track record. But (A) overstates him: 'infallible' is far more than 'others wouldn't do better.'

choices.note: Tempting, because Haddad's whole case is the staff's accomplishments. But 'infallible' is too strong. Haddad says only that others wouldn't choose better. A merely good committee fits his argument fine.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dr. Ruiz has won every award, so she can't have misjudged a single grant.

choices.note: Haddad uses the best-known discoveries only as evidence of good selection; he doesn't need them to be the most important. Not his flaw.
CORRECT. Ostrova objects to how narrowly the committee is drawn. Haddad responds as if she wanted less capable astronomers making the picks, and attacks that.
Haddad offers positive evidence (past discoveries), not a mere lack of disproof. Not an absence-of-evidence argument.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the committee made bad choices, so its choices were sound.

choices.note: Haddad draws no conclusion about all the staff; he talks only about the senior staff on the committee.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our senior chefs are brilliant, so every cook in the kitchen is.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Authority, Ad Hominem, Possible vs. Certain, Part vs. Whole

questions.stimulus: Renovation columnist: Delia Ormond, whose kitchen designs have won several national awards, recently advised homeowners not to install a vapor barrier when finishing a basement, saying that such barriers trap moisture inside the walls and encourage mold. Given Ormond's reputation, homeowners who are finishing their basements this year should follow her advice and leave the vapor barrier out.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about all basements from the experiences of a small number of homeowners in the area
presumes, without providing justification, that what is true of kitchens is also true of basements
attacks the motives of builders who routinely install vapor barriers rather than addressing the reasons they give
treats a person's expertise in one area as a reason to accept her advice about a matter in a different area
fails to consider that some homeowners may not be able to afford to finish their basements this year
questions.explanation: Bad authority: Ormond's awards are for kitchen design, but whether a vapor barrier traps moisture is a building-science question, so her reputation gives no real support to the advice. D says exactly this. B is the tempting trap because kitchens are mentioned, but the argument never reasons from kitchens to basements; kitchens only describe where Ormond's fame comes from.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Homeowners finishing basements this year should leave out the vapor barrier.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Delia Ormond, an award-winning kitchen designer, says vapor barriers trap moisture in basement walls.

breakdown.analysis: So what if she designs beautiful kitchens? Whether a vapor barrier traps moisture is a building-science question, not a design question. The columnist's only support is Ormond's reputation, and that reputation was earned somewhere else. It's like taking a famous pastry chef's word on how to rewire your fuse box. We need an answer that says the argument leans on an expert outside her field. This is the classic appeal to inappropriate authority. Know it.

choices.note: No sample here. The argument doesn't cite any homeowners' experiences at all. Its only evidence is one person's say-so.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Three of my neighbors skipped the vapor barrier and had no problems, so no basement needs one.

choices.note: Tempting, because kitchens come up. But kitchens only explain why Ormond is famous. The argument never says 'this works in kitchens, so it works in basements.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: Tile floors hold up well in kitchens, so they'll hold up well in basements too.

choices.note: The columnist never mentions builders, let alone their motives. That's ad hominem, and it isn't here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Builders who install vapor barriers just want to pad their bills, so ignore what they say about moisture.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ormond's credentials are in kitchen design. The question is moisture control in basement walls. The argument treats her standing in one area as a reason to trust her in another, where it doesn't count.
Irrelevant. The advice is only for people who are finishing basements. Whether others can afford to doesn't touch the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Winery owner: To win more medals for our white wines at the Larkmoor regional competition, we should age them in steel tanks rather than oak barrels. Teodor Vasko, who has judged at Larkmoor for twenty years, insists that steel-aged whites taste fresher and that the Larkmoor judges reward freshness above everything else. No one knows those judges' preferences better than Vasko, so switching to steel is clearly our best course.
