questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the winery owner's argument?
choices: Vasko has judged only red wines at Larkmoor, where white wines are scored by an entirely separate panel.
Some white wines aged in oak barrels have won top medals at several competitions other than Larkmoor.
Many people who regularly buy white wine say they prefer the flavor of whites aged in oak barrels.
Steel tanks cost considerably more to buy and install than the oak barrels the winery now uses.
The written guidelines given to Larkmoor judges list freshness alongside several other qualities that the judges are to consider.
questions.explanation: The plan rests entirely on Vasko's authority about what Larkmoor's judges reward. A shows his experience is with a different panel, so he has no special insight into how whites are scored, and the argument loses its only support. E is the tempting trap, but a list of several qualities is fully compatible with the judges caring about freshness most in practice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching white-wine aging from oak to steel is the best way to win more Larkmoor medals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Vasko, a Larkmoor judge for twenty years, says steel-aged whites taste fresher and that the judges reward freshness most; no one knows the judges better.

breakdown.analysis: Everything hangs on Vasko. Why should we believe him about how whites are judged? Because he's judged at Larkmoor for twenty years. But judged what, exactly? If his experience doesn't actually cover the white-wine panel, his 'insider knowledge' is just an opinion. We want an answer that cuts Vasko's expertise off from the specific question. Weakening an appeal to authority often works this way: you don't attack the claim, you show the authority isn't an authority on it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Vasko's twenty years are all on the red-wine side, and whites go to a different panel. So he has no special knowledge of what the white-wine judges reward, and the argument's only support collapses.
Other competitions are irrelevant. The argument is only about Larkmoor's judges.
Wrong group. The owner wants to please Larkmoor judges, not ordinary buyers.
Wrong dimension. The goal is medals, not saving money. A costly plan can still be the best way to win medals.
Tempting. It seems to dent 'above everything else.' But a guideline listing several qualities says nothing about which one the judges actually weight most. Freshness could still dominate in practice.

questions.stimulus: Some staff pharmacists at a regional hospital have objected that the hospital's new protocol for tapering patients off sedatives is too rapid and will cause withdrawal symptoms. In response, a hospital spokesperson noted that the protocol was reviewed and unanimously approved by the board of trustees, a group that includes several of the region's most accomplished business executives and attorneys, and concluded that the pharmacists' objection can be set aside.
questions.stem: The spokesperson's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that a tapering schedule that is rapid cannot also be safe for the patients who are placed on it
dismisses the pharmacists' objection on the grounds that pharmacists have a professional stake in how sedatives are prescribed
fails to consider that the protocol might produce side effects other than withdrawal symptoms in some of the patients
infers that the pharmacists' objection is mistaken merely because no one has yet shown that it is correct
treats a group's approval as settling a question that its members have not been shown to be competent to judge
questions.explanation: The spokesperson's only answer to the pharmacists is that the trustees approved the protocol, but the trustees are distinguished in business and law, not pharmacology, so their approval says nothing about withdrawal risk. (E) says this without naming the trustees or the field. Most students pick (B), because the spokesperson is brushing off critics and that smells like an attack on the source; but nothing is said about the pharmacists' interests or motives: the argument appeals to an unqualified group rather than attacking a qualified one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The pharmacists' objection can be set aside.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The protocol was unanimously approved by the board of trustees, which includes accomplished business executives and attorneys.

breakdown.analysis: Who approved the protocol? Executives and lawyers. Who objected? Pharmacists, the people who actually know how sedative withdrawal works. The spokesperson answers a pharmacology question with the votes of people who aren't shown to know any pharmacology. It's like settling a dispute about your car's brakes by noting that your accountant approved them. Prephrase: the argument relies on a group whose expertise doesn't cover the question. The correct answer says this in the abstract ('a group,' 'its members'), so you have to map it back. Most students pick (B), because 'dismissing critics' sounds like ad hominem. But the spokesperson never says a word about the pharmacists themselves.

choices.note: That's the pharmacists' worry, not something the spokesperson takes for granted. The spokesperson never discusses speed or safety at all.

Tempting, because the spokesperson waves away critics. But the argument never mentions the pharmacists' interests, motives or careers. It props up the protocol with another group's approval; it doesn't attack the objectors.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The pharmacists only object because the protocol means more paperwork for them, so ignore them.

choices.note: Other side effects would be another objection, not a flaw in the spokesperson's reasoning about this one.
The spokesperson doesn't argue from lack of proof. She offers positive (if worthless) support: the board's approval.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the new schedule causes withdrawal, so it doesn't.

choices.note: CORRECT. The board's members are distinguished in business and law, not pharmacology. Their unanimous approval is treated as settling a pharmacological question they aren't shown to be competent to judge.

questions.stimulus: Lena Corvo has anchored the evening news on Channel 6 for fifteen years, and in surveys the city's viewers consistently name her the most trustworthy broadcaster in the city. Corvo recently said on the air that the city's proposed transit tax would drive many small businesses out of the downtown area. So the transit tax would drive many small businesses out of the downtown area.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Ruth Avila has inspected bridges for the state for twenty years, and her colleagues consistently call her the most reliable engineer they know. She has concluded that the Arlen River bridge needs new supports. So the Arlen River bridge needs new supports.

Dr. Imes is the most accomplished heart surgeon at Linden Hospital, and her patients consistently rate her the most trustworthy physician there. She has said that the hospital's new billing software will raise its costs. So the software will raise the hospital's costs.

Gerta Haan is the region's most respected wine critic, and readers say they trust her reviews above all others. She has called the Ostler vineyard's newest red undrinkable. So the Ostler vineyard will not sell much of its newest red.

The novelist Hugo Rane has written many bestselling mysteries, but reviewers agree that his grasp of economics is weak. So the claims he makes in his recent magazine essay on international trade policy must all be false.

Most residents of Garvin, including several who have lived there for decades, believe that the town's old mill is unsafe to enter. So the old mill is probably unsafe to enter, and the town council should close it to the public.
questions.explanation: The stimulus accepts a claim about economics because the person making it is trusted and accomplished in an unrelated field, broadcasting. (B) does the same, and hides it well: a heart surgeon's skill and her patients' trust are taken to settle a question about billing software, with the shared hospital setting masking the change of field. Most students pick (A), because it matches the stimulus's surface most closely (long tenure, a trust rating, a claim, 'so it's true'); but Avila is a bridge inspector speaking about a bridge, so her expertise covers the claim and the stimulus's flaw is absent.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The transit tax would drive many small businesses out of downtown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corvo has anchored the news for fifteen years and viewers rate her the most trustworthy broadcaster; she said the tax would do this.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A person is trusted and accomplished in field X; she makes a claim about field Y; so the claim is true.

breakdown.analysis: What does reading the news have to do with predicting how a tax affects small businesses? Nothing. Being trusted to read the headlines isn't expertise in economics. The flaw is the field mismatch, not the mere appeal to a person. It's like trusting your dentist's stock tips because she does great fillings. Prephrase: an argument that accepts a claim because its source is respected in some other field. Most students pick (A), because it copies the structure (tenure, trust rating, claim, conclusion). But Avila's field is the claim's field. Same skeleton with the flaw removed is the classic parallel-flaw trap.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a near-copy of the stimulus's structure. But a veteran bridge inspector judging a bridge is speaking inside her expertise. Without the field mismatch, the stimulus's flaw is gone.

CORRECT. Imes's accomplishments and patients' trust are in heart surgery; her claim is about software costs. The shared hospital setting disguises it, but it's the same move: skill in one field used to settle a question in another.
Haan is judging wine, which is her field. The leap here is from her opinion to sales figures, a different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The top food critic hated the new diner, so it will go out of business.

choices.note: The reverse move: it rejects claims because the author lacks expertise, concluding they're false. Lack of expertise doesn't make a claim false, but that's not the stimulus's flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My uncle isn't a doctor, so his advice to drink water must be wrong.

choices.note: An appeal to popular opinion, plus an added recommendation. No one's expertise in one field is transferred to another.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most people think this bridge is safe, so it is.

questions.stimulus: Greenhouse manager: Our Cassel orchids have begun to wilt. Dr. Mira Tesh, who has spent thirty years studying Cassel orchids in the cloud forests where they grow wild, says that when a Cassel orchid wilts, the cause is almost always too much water. Since no one knows Cassel orchids better than Dr. Tesh, our orchids are probably being overwatered, and we should water them less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the greenhouse manager's argument?
choices: Dr. Tesh has observed at least one Cassel orchid growing in a greenhouse that wilted because it had been overwatered.
Most botanists who study orchids accept Dr. Tesh's claim about what usually causes Cassel orchids to wilt in the wild.
Why Cassel orchids wilt in the wild is at least some guide to why they wilt in greenhouses.
Cassel orchids grown in greenhouses wilt for exactly the same reasons as do Cassel orchids growing in the wild.
Watering the greenhouse's Cassel orchids less than they are now watered will not cause them any harm at all.
questions.explanation: Tesh's authority comes entirely from studying wild orchids, so the manager must assume her knowledge carries over at least somewhat to greenhouse orchids; if wild wilting tells us nothing about greenhouse wilting, her say-so is irrelevant. (C) states this modestly. Most students pick (D), because it is exactly the gap a quick prephrase names; but it is the right idea at the wrong strength: the manager concludes only that overwatering is 'probably' the cause, so the reasons need not be exactly the same, and negating (D) leaves the argument standing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Our orchids are probably being overwatered, so we should water them less.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dr. Tesh, who has studied wild Cassel orchids for thirty years, says wilting is almost always caused by too much water; no one knows the plant better.

breakdown.analysis: Tesh is an expert, but on what? Wild orchids in cloud forests. The manager's orchids live in a greenhouse, where watering, light and soil are all controlled. If wild wilting tells us nothing about greenhouse wilting, Tesh's rule doesn't apply. It's like asking a wolf expert why your poodle is limping. Prephrase: what holds for wild orchids is at least some guide to greenhouse orchids. Keep it modest: the conclusion says 'probably.' Most students pick (D), because it names the transfer directly. But 'exactly the same reasons' is far more than the argument needs.

choices.note: Would make Tesh more convincing, but isn't required. Her wild-orchid knowledge can carry over even if she's never seen a greenhouse case. Negate it and the argument still works.
choices.negation: Dr. Tesh has never observed a Cassel orchid growing in a greenhouse that wilted because it had been overwatered.

choices.note: Other botanists' agreement would add support but isn't needed. Negate it and Tesh's knowledge could still be right and still carry over.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most botanists who study orchids accept Dr. Tesh's claim about what usually causes Cassel orchids to wilt in the wild.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: why they wilt in the wild is no guide at all to why they wilt in greenhouses. Then Tesh's expertise is beside the point and nothing supports 'probably overwatered.'
choices.negation: Why Cassel orchids wilt in the wild is no guide at all to why they wilt in greenhouses.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the right gap. But too strong. Negate it: greenhouse orchids don't wilt for exactly the same reasons (maybe a few causes differ). Wild patterns can still be a decent guide, and 'probably overwatered' survives.
choices.negation: Cassel orchids grown in greenhouses do not wilt for exactly the same reasons as do Cassel orchids growing in the wild.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: watering less would cause some harm. If the plants are drowning, a little harm may still be worth it. The recommendation survives.
choices.negation: Watering the greenhouse's Cassel orchids less than they are now watered will cause them at least some harm.

questions.stimulus: Labor economist Rhea Dalton argues that the province's proposed ban on noncompete agreements would raise wages for warehouse workers, because employers would then have to compete harder to keep the workers they have. But Dalton has spent most of her career as a paid consultant to labor unions, which have long campaigned for such a ban. Her argument should therefore be rejected.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about all workers in the province from evidence concerning only the province's warehouse workers
presumes, without providing justification, that the proposed ban would not raise wages for any warehouse workers
relies on the testimony of an economist about a matter that lies outside her area of expertise
fails to consider that some employers in the province might actually benefit from a ban on noncompete agreements
treats facts about the person who advances an argument as sufficient grounds for rejecting that argument
questions.explanation: Ad hominem: Dalton gives a reason (employers would have to compete to keep workers), but the argument ignores that reason and rejects her case because she has worked for unions. E describes this. B is the tempting trap, but the argument concludes only that Dalton's argument should be rejected; it never asserts that wages would not rise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dalton's argument that the noncompete ban would raise warehouse wages should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dalton has long been a paid consultant to unions, which support the ban.

breakdown.analysis: Dalton gave a real reason: without noncompetes, employers have to compete to keep workers. Did the arguer say anything about that reason? No. It just points at who has paid her. Her ties to unions might be a reason to check her work carefully, but they don't make her reasoning wrong. This is the ad hominem (circumstantial) flaw. Know it.

choices.note: The argument only discusses warehouse workers. It doesn't generalize to all workers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Warehouse wages rose after the ban, so every worker's wages will rise.

choices.note: Tempting, but the argument stops at 'reject her argument.' It never claims wages won't rise. Rejecting someone's argument isn't the same as asserting the opposite.
Dalton is a labor economist talking about wages. That's squarely her field. No inappropriate authority here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous tenor says the ban will raise wages, so it will.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether some employers benefit has nothing to do with the move from Dalton's background to rejecting her argument.

CORRECT. The argument rejects Dalton's case because of who has paid her, never engaging her actual reason about employers competing for workers. A fact about the arguer is treated as grounds for rejecting the argument.

questions.stimulus: Kwame has proposed that his software team stop requiring a second reviewer for code changes of under twenty lines, arguing that such reviews delay releases far more than they improve quality. The team's manager rejected the proposal on the grounds that Kwame is the team member who has most often been criticized for submitting careless code.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the manager's argument depends?
choices: Second reviews of small code changes improve the quality of code more than they delay the team's releases.
No other member of the software team has publicly expressed support for Kwame's proposal to drop second reviews.
Kwame's record of careless code is at least some reason to doubt the merits of his proposal.
Team members who have been criticized for careless code produce more errors than any of the team's other members.
Kwame made his proposal primarily in order to avoid any further criticism of the code that he submits.
questions.explanation: The manager rejects the proposal solely because of Kwame's record, so the argument requires that his record has some bearing on whether the proposal is any good; negate C and the only reason for rejection disappears. E is the tempting trap: a self-serving motive would help the manager, but the argument can stand on Kwame's record without any claim about why he made the proposal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kwame's proposal to drop second reviews for small code changes should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kwame is the team member most often criticized for careless code.

breakdown.analysis: Kwame offered a reason: small-change reviews cost more time than they're worth. The manager ignores it and points to Kwame's track record. For that to count as a reason to reject the proposal, the manager has to assume that who Kwame is tells us something about whether his idea is good. That's the hidden premise in every ad hominem. Prephrase: Kwame's record bears on the merits of his proposal.

choices.note: Tempting, since it supports the conclusion. But the manager's argument doesn't rest on any claim about what reviews actually do. Negate it (reviews don't improve quality more than they delay) and the manager's reasoning, which is all about Kwame, isn't touched.
choices.negation: Second reviews of small code changes do not improve the quality of code more than they delay the team's releases.

choices.note: Not required. Others could back Kwame and the manager could still reject the idea on the stated grounds. Negate it and nothing breaks.
choices.negation: At least one other member of the software team has publicly expressed support for Kwame's proposal.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Kwame's record gives no reason at all to doubt his proposal. Then the manager's only reason for rejecting it is gone. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Kwame's record of careless code gives no reason at all to doubt the merits of his proposal.

choices.note: Too strong ('more than any other'). The argument doesn't need a ranking of error rates. Negate it and the reasoning is unaffected.
choices.negation: Team members who have been criticized for careless code do not produce more errors than all of the team's other members.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like what the manager is hinting at. But the argument never mentions motives; it relies on his record. Negate it (avoiding criticism wasn't his main reason) and the manager can still lean on the record.
choices.negation: Kwame did not make his proposal primarily in order to avoid any further criticism of the code that he submits.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Several scholars have argued that the Varrian inscriptions, which celebrate the victories of King Osric, were carved centuries after his reign. But every one of these scholars trained at Delmont University, whose faculty has long been hostile to work that glorifies Osric. So their dating should be disregarded, and the inscriptions most likely date from Osric's own reign.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?
choices: The scholars base their dating on a style of lettering that appears only in texts produced long after Osric's reign.
Several scholars with no connection to Delmont University doubt that the inscriptions give an accurate account of Osric's victories.
Delmont University's faculty has published several studies praising rulers who reigned in the region in the centuries before Osric.
In the region, inscriptions celebrating a king's victories were usually carved while that king was still alive and able to see them.
The historian has written a popular book that portrays Osric's reign and military campaigns in an extremely favorable light.
questions.explanation: The historian dismisses the late dating by pointing to the scholars' training and supposed bias, never to their evidence. (A) shows that the dating rests on evidence that stands regardless of anyone's motives, so the attack on the scholars leaves it intact. Most students pick (B), because it seems to show that skepticism exists beyond Delmont; but those outside scholars doubt the inscriptions' accuracy, not their date, a one-word scope swap. (E) only turns the same kind of attack on the historian.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The late dating should be disregarded; the inscriptions most likely date from Osric's reign.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every scholar proposing the late date trained at Delmont, whose faculty has long been hostile to work glorifying Osric.

breakdown.analysis: So what if they trained at Delmont? Bias can make you look for evidence; it doesn't make the evidence disappear. The historian never says what the scholars' reasons are, only where they went to school. That's ad hominem: attacking the source instead of the argument. It's like rejecting a thermometer reading because the person holding it hates summer. To weaken, show the late date rests on evidence that holds up whoever presents it. Most students pick (B), since 'scholars outside Delmont doubt the inscriptions' sounds like independent support for the late date. Read the object: they doubt the account's accuracy, not when it was carved.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the dating rests on letter forms found only in much later texts, the evidence speaks for itself. Whatever the scholars' leanings, the inscriptions look late, and dismissing them for their training is exposed as beside the point.

Tempting, because it suggests the doubters aren't all from Delmont. But these scholars doubt whether the inscriptions are accurate, not when they were carved. An accurate or inaccurate boast can be carved in Osric's lifetime either way.
Praising earlier rulers doesn't show the faculty isn't hostile to Osric; if anything it fits a preference for other kings. It doesn't touch the dating evidence.
This supports the historian: if victory inscriptions were usually carved during the king's life, an early date looks more likely. Wrong direction.
An attack on the historian's motives. That's the same mistake the historian made; it doesn't show the historian's conclusion is wrong.

questions.stimulus: Station manager: Corbin, our weather forecaster, claims that the station's new radar software regularly misreports rainfall totals, sometimes by more than an inch. But Corbin was passed over for promotion to chief meteorologist shortly after the software was installed, and he has resented the station's management ever since. Therefore, his claim about the software is false.
questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the station manager's argument?
choices: Garza claims that the old footbridge in Wilton Park needs extensive repair. But Garza is a schoolteacher, not an engineer, and she has never inspected a bridge. So we have no good reason to believe that the footbridge needs extensive repair.

Ines says that the new vaccine her company makes is safe, and she clearly stands to gain if it sells well. But Ines bases her claim on large independent trials that her company did not fund. So her claim is probably true.

Pratt maintains that Selwyn's new novel is overrated. But Pratt has publicly disliked every one of Selwyn's earlier novels, often in harsh terms. So Pratt's opinion of the new novel probably reflects that long-standing dislike rather than the novel's merits.

Hollis contends that the county's new zoning code is unconstitutional. But Hollis owns land whose value fell sharply when the code took effect, and he has opposed the code ever since. Therefore, the code does not violate the constitution.

Ruiz argues that the city should build a new park in the downtown area. But proposals for downtown parks have failed to win council approval several times in the past. Therefore, Ruiz's proposal will also fail to win approval.
questions.explanation: The manager concludes that Corbin's claim is false because Corbin has a grievance, moving from a person's motive to the falsity of what he says. (D) matches, with its conclusion restated ('does not violate the constitution' rather than 'the claim is false'). Most students pick (C), because it also cites a critic's personal history with his target; but (C) concludes only that Pratt's opinion probably reflects his dislike, a claim about where the opinion comes from, which is reasonable, not that the novel isn't overrated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corbin's claim about the radar software is false.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corbin was passed over for promotion after the software was installed and has resented management since.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Person P claims X; P has a personal grievance related to X; so X is false.

breakdown.analysis: Does a grudge make a claim false? No. Corbin might be bitter and still right about the rainfall numbers. The manager goes from 'he has a motive' all the way to 'his claim is false.' That's ad hominem, and the strong conclusion ('false') is part of the pattern. It's like saying a fired cashier's report of missing money must be wrong because she's angry. Prephrase: someone with a grievance makes a claim, so the claim is false. Watch the strength: an answer that ends with 'probably colored by bias' isn't the same as 'false.' Most students pick (C) for that reason.

choices.note: An argument about lack of expertise, and it concludes only that we lack reason to believe the claim, not that it's false. Different flaw, weaker conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: You're not a chef, so your complaint that the soup is cold must be wrong.

choices.note: Reasonable: it notes a motive but then points to independent evidence. Not flawed in the stimulus's way.

Tempting, because it cites a critic's history with his target. But it concludes only that Pratt's opinion probably reflects dislike. That's a modest claim about the opinion's source, not a verdict that the novel isn't overrated.
CORRECT. Hollis's financial grievance is taken to show his claim is false (the code is constitutional). Same move from motive to falsity, just with the conclusion restated.
Reasoning from past outcomes to a prediction. Nothing about the arguer's motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The last three bake sales lost money, so this one will too.

questions.stimulus: Several vintners in the Osterlund region have endorsed winemaker Jonas Ferrier's recommendation that vines in the region not be irrigated, accepting his claim that irrigation dilutes the flavor of the grapes. Yet Ferrier's own vineyard has been irrigated every summer for the past decade, as anyone driving past it can see. Osterlund's vintners should therefore disregard his recommendation and keep irrigating their vines.
questions.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: relies on the judgment of an authority whose expertise lies outside the particular matter at issue
treats a fact about the person offering a reason for a recommendation as showing that the reason is unsound
fails to consider that irrigation might affect qualities of the grapes other than their flavor, such as their size or sugar content
presumes, without providing justification, that the conditions in Ferrier's vineyard are typical of those in every other vineyard in the region
takes for granted that the vintners who endorsed the recommendation did so solely because of Ferrier's reputation
questions.explanation: Ferrier gave a reason (irrigation dilutes flavor), and the argument dismisses it because Ferrier himself irrigates, a fact about him rather than about his reason. (B) states this abstractly. Most students pick (D), because a single vineyard seems to be standing in for the region; but the argument never uses Ferrier's vineyard as evidence about other vineyards. It uses his conduct only to discredit him.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Osterlund's vintners should disregard Ferrier's recommendation and keep irrigating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ferrier recommends no irrigation because it dilutes flavor; Ferrier's own vineyard is irrigated every summer.

breakdown.analysis: So Ferrier doesn't follow his own advice. Does that make irrigation stop diluting flavor? No. Maybe he values yield over flavor, or maybe he's a hypocrite. Either way his reason is untouched. Dismissing an argument because the arguer doesn't practice it is called tu quoque, a form of ad hominem. It's a classic; know it. It's like ignoring a smoker who tells you smoking causes cancer. Prephrase: rejects a reason because of a fact about the person giving it. Most students pick (D), because Ferrier's vineyard looks like a sample of one. But nothing about the region is inferred from that vineyard.

choices.note: Ferrier is a winemaker talking about grapes, so this isn't an out-of-field appeal. And the argument rejects his judgment rather than relying on it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous chef says this bridge is safe, so it is.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ferrier's habit of irrigating is a fact about him. The argument treats it as showing his reason (irrigation dilutes flavor) is wrong. That's the tu quoque move.
Other qualities like size don't matter to the flaw. The argument rejects the flavor reason without engaging it at all.
Tempting, because one vineyard and a whole region both appear. But the argument doesn't say 'what happens at Ferrier's applies everywhere.' His vineyard is used only to make him look inconsistent.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Irrigation works fine at my vineyard, so it works at every vineyard in the region.

choices.note: The argument doesn't care why the other vintners endorsed the advice. It says they should drop it because of Ferrier's conduct.

questions.stimulus: Gardener: The new Kestrow fertilizer has become popular because it makes flowering plants bloom earlier. But it contains a compound that can stunt root growth in young ferns. This spring, the botanical garden's staff treated all of its fern beds, including the beds of newly planted ferns, with Kestrow. So the young ferns in the garden will have stunted roots this year.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the gardener's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: mistakes what may be an effect of stunted root growth in young ferns for the cause of that stunting
fails to consider that young ferns might be harmed by compounds other than the one contained in Kestrow
takes for granted that what can stunt young ferns' roots will in fact stunt these ferns' roots
presumes, without providing justification, that what is true of young ferns is also true of the garden's mature ferns
draws a conclusion about all ferns from a sample of ferns that may not be representative of ferns in general
questions.explanation: The premise says the compound can stunt roots; the conclusion says the ferns will have stunted roots. That jump from possible to certain is the flaw, and C names it. B is the tempting trap because 'fails to consider other causes' is a common flaw, but other harmful compounds would not undercut the prediction; the problem is that this compound may not stunt these ferns at all.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The garden's young ferns will have stunted roots this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kestrow contains a compound that can stunt root growth in young ferns; the fern beds were treated with Kestrow.

breakdown.analysis: 'Can' isn't 'will.' Lots of things can harm you without actually doing so: the dose may be too small, the conditions may be wrong, the ferns may tolerate it. The gardener turns a possibility into a certainty. Watch for this switch between 'can/may' in a premise and 'will/must' in a conclusion. We need an answer that says the argument treats a possible effect as a sure one.

choices.note: No reversal here. The argument says the compound causes stunting, not that stunting causes something else.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ferns with stunted roots get less water, so lack of water must be what stunts their roots.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'ignores other causes' is a classic flaw. But other compounds would only make stunting more likely. The real problem is that this compound might not stunt these ferns at all.
CORRECT. The compound can stunt roots; the gardener takes for granted that it will stunt these roots. That's a possibility treated as a certainty.
The argument never mentions mature ferns. Its conclusion is about young ferns only.
The conclusion is about the ferns in this garden, the very ferns that were treated. No sample is being generalized.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The ferns in one bed were stunted, so every fern in the region will be.

questions.stimulus: Under the new labor contract at a packaging plant, if the plant's monthly orders fall below 40,000 units for two consecutive months, the plant's night shift will be eliminated. Orders fell below 40,000 units last month, and the company's own forecasts show that they could do so again this month. A union representative concluded from this that the night shift will certainly be eliminated.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the union representative's argument?
choices: The company's forecasts of monthly orders have occasionally been less accurate than the forecasts of independent analysts.
Under the contract, workers whose shift is eliminated must be offered positions on the plant's remaining day and evening shifts.
Orders at the plant fell below 40,000 units in several separate months before the new contract took effect.
The contract also permits the company to eliminate the night shift for reasons unrelated to the volume of orders.
The same forecasts indicate that orders this month will very probably exceed 45,000 units by a wide margin.
questions.explanation: The contract's condition is sufficient for eliminating the shift, so the shift goes if orders fall short again; but the forecasts say only that this could happen, and the representative concludes it certainly will. E shows the shortfall is unlikely, which directly undercuts the certainty. A is the tempting trap, but occasional inaccuracy cuts both ways and does not make a second shortfall any less likely.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The night shift will certainly be eliminated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Below 40,000 for two straight months → night shift eliminated; below 40,000 last month; forecasts say orders could fall below 40,000 this month.

breakdown.analysis: The rule: two months in a row under 40,000 → shift eliminated. One month is done. The second month is only a 'could.' So the conclusion 'certainly' depends on something that's merely possible. What weakens this? Anything showing that a second bad month is unlikely. Then the sufficient condition probably won't be met, and the certainty evaporates.

choices.note: Tempting, because it casts doubt on the forecasts. But 'occasionally less accurate' doesn't say which way they err. It doesn't make a shortfall any less likely, so it doesn't attack the certainty.
So? This is about what happens to workers after the shift is gone. It doesn't affect whether the shift is eliminated.
Irrelevant. Shortfalls before the contract don't count toward its two-month trigger, and they say little about this month.
Opposite direction. More ways to eliminate the shift makes elimination more likely, if anything.

CORRECT. The same forecasts that show a shortfall is possible show it's unlikely; orders will very probably top 45,000. Then the second bad month probably won't happen, and 'certainly eliminated' is badly overstated.

questions.stimulus: The antibiotic Corvilex is effective against most common respiratory infections, but it can cause dizziness in patients who are also taking medication for high blood pressure. Mr. Alvar has just been prescribed a ten-day course of Corvilex for a sinus infection, and he takes medication daily for high blood pressure. Therefore, Mr. Alvar will experience dizziness during his treatment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Heavy rain in the hills can cause the Lund River to flood the low-lying farms along its banks. The Lund River flooded those farms last week. Therefore, there must have been heavy rain in the hills near the Lund River last week.

The library's saved files are going to be corrupted. After all, every one of the library's computers runs an older operating system, and last night each of them received a software update that can corrupt saved files on such computers.

Frost kills any tomato seedling that is left uncovered overnight in early spring. The seedlings in the garden's north bed were left uncovered last night, and there was a hard frost. Therefore, the seedlings in the north bed are now dead.

A certain pesticide kills aphids only when it is applied in warm weather. The pesticide was applied to the Ortega field during last month's cold spell. Therefore, the aphids in the Ortega field survived the application and are still damaging the crop.

Dogs that are left alone for long periods often become anxious and destructive. Ms. Rook's dog is regularly left alone for most of the day while she works. Therefore, Ms. Rook's dog is probably at least somewhat anxious.
questions.explanation: The stimulus moves from 'X can cause Y under condition C' and 'this case meets C' to 'Y will happen,' treating a possibility as a certainty. (B) has exactly that structure, though it states its conclusion first. Most students pick (E), because it has the same can-happen-here skeleton; but (E) starts from 'often' and concludes only 'probably,' which is a reasonable inference. (C) is valid because frost kills any uncovered seedling.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mr. Alvar will experience dizziness during his treatment.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corvilex can cause dizziness in patients on blood-pressure medication; Alvar is taking both.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X can cause Y under condition C; this case meets C; so Y will happen.

breakdown.analysis: 'Can cause' isn't 'will cause.' Lots of people on both drugs might never get dizzy. The argument turns a risk into a certainty. It's like saying wet roads can cause crashes, it's raining, so you will crash. Prephrase: can-cause plus the condition, concluding will-happen. Match the certainty level, not just the topic. Most students pick (E), because its skeleton is the same. But (E)'s conclusion is hedged ('probably,' 'at least somewhat'), so it matches its 'often' premise. The order of sentences doesn't matter: (B) puts its conclusion first.

choices.note: Reverses the reasoning: heavy rain can cause floods; there was a flood; so there was heavy rain. That's inferring a cause from an effect that has other possible causes.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Burnt toast can set off the smoke alarm. The alarm went off. So someone burnt toast.

choices.note: CORRECT. The update 'can corrupt' files on older systems; the library's computers are older and got the update; so files 'are going to be' corrupted. Possibility treated as certainty, with the conclusion stated first.
Valid. 'Kills any' seedling left uncovered is a guarantee, not a possibility, so the conclusion follows.
A different structure: a necessary condition for the pesticide working (warm weather) wasn't met, so it didn't work, plus an extra claim about crop damage. Not possibility-to-certainty.
Tempting, because the skeleton matches. But 'often' leads only to 'probably at least somewhat anxious.' The conclusion's strength matches the premise, so this one is reasonable.

questions.stimulus: Termites can enter a house through any wooden structure that is in direct contact with the soil. After examining the Pell house, a building inspector noted that the wooden posts supporting its back porch rest directly on bare soil. She concluded that unless those posts are raised onto concrete footings, the Pell house will become infested with termites.
questions.stem: The inspector's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Termites either are already present or at some time will be present in the soil near the Pell house.
Raising the porch posts onto concrete footings would prevent all termite damage to every part of the Pell house.
Termites cannot enter a house except through wooden structures that are in direct contact with the soil.
The Pell house has been infested with termites at least once at some time in the past.
Termites generally do more damage to porches than they do to any other part of a house.
questions.explanation: The premise establishes only that termites can get in through the posts; to conclude the house will be infested, the inspector must assume termites are, or will be, around to use that route. Negate (A) and infestation becomes impossible. Most students pick (C), because it seems to make the posts the crucial issue; but if termites had other ways in, infestation would be more likely, not less, so the argument does not need (C). (B) reverses the 'unless' conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless the porch posts are raised onto concrete footings, the Pell house will become infested.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Termites can enter through any wood touching the soil; the Pell porch posts rest on bare soil.

breakdown.analysis: The posts give termites a way in. But a door isn't a visitor. If there are no termites in the area, now or ever, an open path doesn't matter. The inspector moves from 'termites can get in' to 'termites will get in,' so she needs, at minimum, termites that will actually be around to use that path. Prephrase: there are, or will be, termites near the house. Note how modest the right answer is: not 'many termites,' not 'termites now.' Most students pick (C), because 'the posts are the only way in' feels like what the inspector is banking on. Negate it, though, and more entry routes only make infestation likelier.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: there are no termites near the Pell house and there never will be. Then nothing can come through the posts, and the prediction of infestation falls apart.
choices.negation: Termites are not present in the soil near the Pell house, and they never will be.

choices.note: This reverses the conditional. The inspector's claim is: posts not raised → infestation. It says nothing about raising them guaranteeing safety. Negate (B) and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Raising the porch posts onto concrete footings would not prevent all termite damage to every part of the Pell house.

choices.note: Tempting, since it seems to make the posts the key issue. But negate it: termites can also get in other ways. That makes infestation more likely, not less. The argument doesn't need the posts to be the only route.
choices.negation: Termites can enter a house in at least one way other than through wooden structures in direct contact with the soil.

choices.note: Not needed. A house can be infested for the first time. Negate it (never infested before) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: The Pell house has never been infested with termites.

choices.note: Irrelevant ranking. The argument is about whether infestation happens, not where termites do the most damage.
choices.negation: It is not the case that termites generally do more damage to porches than to any other part of a house.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Some historians maintain that the bronze tools found at the ancient settlement of Orvane must have been imported, since no tin deposits have been found anywhere near the site. But chemical analysis of every one of the tools shows that their tin matches that of a small deposit, discovered only last year, in hills thirty kilometers from Orvane. Thus the tools were made at Orvane, and the historians are mistaken.
questions.stem: The archaeologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: relies on a chemical analysis without establishing that the people who performed it were qualified to do so
rejects the historians' position by attacking their motives rather than by addressing the evidence they cite
treats the absence of evidence that tin deposits existed near Orvane as proof that none existed
treats evidence that merely removes an obstacle to a hypothesis as though it established that the hypothesis is true
draws a conclusion about all of the bronze tools found at Orvane from an analysis of only some of those tools
questions.explanation: The historians' reason for 'imported' was that there was no nearby tin; the new deposit removes that obstacle, showing local manufacture was possible. But the archaeologist concludes the tools were made at Orvane, though the tin could have been carried elsewhere, worked there, and the tools brought back. (D) describes this possible-to-actual move abstractly. Most students pick (C), because an absence-of-evidence flaw really is in the passage; but it is the historians' flaw, not the archaeologist's.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Orvane tools were made at Orvane; the historians are mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The historians said 'imported' because no tin was found nearby; analysis of every tool matches its tin to a newly found deposit thirty kilometers away.

breakdown.analysis: The new deposit knocks out the historians' reason. Fine. But what does it prove? Only that local manufacture was possible. Tin from those hills could have gone to another town, been cast into tools there, and the tools brought to Orvane. 'Could have been made here' isn't 'was made here.' It's like proving a suspect had a key to the room and concluding he's the thief. Most students pick (C), because they spot the textbook absence-of-evidence move. It's there, but the historians made it. Always check whose reasoning the stem asks about.

choices.note: Nothing suggests the analysts were unqualified, and the problem isn't trust in the lab. It's what the result actually shows.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My neighbor ran the test in his garage and says the tin matches, so it does.

choices.note: The archaeologist never mentions the historians' motives. The response addresses their evidence (no nearby tin) head-on.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Those historians just want to make Orvane look backward, so ignore their dating.

choices.note: Tempting, because there is an absence-of-evidence flaw here: no deposit found, so none existed. But that's the historians' reasoning, and the archaeologist rejects it. The stem asks about the archaeologist.
CORRECT. The tin match removes the obstacle to local manufacture. The archaeologist then treats 'made at Orvane' as established, ignoring that the tin could have been worked somewhere else.
The analysis covered every one of the tools, so there's no some-to-all leap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Two of the ten tools are local, so all ten are.

questions.stimulus: Telquist Software tracks how long each of its engineers takes, on average, to resolve a software defect. By that measure, each of the five engineers on the Velo team is faster than any engineer on the Arden team. Therefore, the Velo team as a whole will clear a large backlog of urgent defects more quickly than the Arden team would, and the backlog should be assigned to Velo.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about all software engineers from a sample consisting of only five engineers
infers that a group has a property from the fact that each of its members has that property
takes for granted that the speed at which defects are resolved is the only measure of a team's quality
confuses a condition that is necessary for resolving defects quickly with one that is sufficient for doing so
fails to consider that the Arden team's engineers may have more years of experience than those on the Velo team
questions.explanation: Part-whole (composition): each Velo engineer is faster than each Arden engineer, but how fast a team clears a backlog also depends on how many engineers it has and how they work together; Arden might have many more engineers. B names this. A is the tempting trap because 'five' sounds like a small sample, but the argument concludes only about these two teams, not about software engineers in general.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Velo team as a whole will clear the urgent backlog faster than Arden would, so Velo should get it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of Velo's five engineers is individually faster than any Arden engineer.

breakdown.analysis: Faster individuals don't guarantee a faster team. What if Arden has twenty engineers and Velo has five? Twenty slower people can still clear more defects than five fast ones. It's like saying every player on a three-person rowing crew is stronger than anyone on an eight-person crew, so the three-person boat is faster. This is the part-to-whole (composition) flaw. Know it.

choices.note: Tempting, because five sounds small. But the conclusion isn't about software engineers in general. It's about these two teams, and the argument has data on every Velo engineer.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Five engineers I surveyed prefer tabs, so most engineers prefer tabs.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each Velo engineer is faster, so the argument concludes the Velo team will be faster. That moves a property of the parts to the whole without justification. Team size alone could reverse the result.
The argument never claims Velo is the better team overall, only that it will clear the backlog faster. No shift to quality.
No conditional is in play. Nothing is stated as necessary or sufficient for quick resolution.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fast teams use code review, and we use code review, so we're fast.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument already gives speed data on each engineer; experience is just one possible reason for speed, and it doesn't touch the jump from individuals to teams.

questions.stimulus: Labor analyst: Some regional officials doubt that the Tarran region's labor market improved at all last year. They are mistaken. Last year, the unemployment rate declined in each of the four counties that make up the Tarran region, in two of them by more than a full percentage point. It follows that the unemployment rate for the Tarran region as a whole also declined last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the labor analyst's argument?
choices: Unemployment rates also declined last year in most of the country's other regions, including those bordering Tarran.
The county with the highest unemployment rate in the Tarran region had the smallest decline in that rate last year.
Several large employers opened new facilities in the Tarran region last year and hired mostly local residents.
The proportion of Tarran's labor force living in each of its four counties barely changed during last year.
Last year, the Tarran region's labor force grew more slowly than the labor force of the country as a whole.
questions.explanation: A region's unemployment rate is an average of its counties' rates weighted by labor-force size, so it can rise even when every county's rate falls if workers shift toward a high-unemployment county. D rules out such a shift, closing the part-to-whole gap. C is the tempting trap because new employers sound like good news, but every county's rate already fell; the question is whether the regional figure follows, and C says nothing about that.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tarran's regional unemployment rate declined last year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The unemployment rate declined in each of Tarran's four counties.

breakdown.analysis: Seems airtight, right? It isn't. A regional rate is a weighted average. Suppose County A has 2 percent unemployment and County B has 12 percent. Both drop a point, to 1 and 11. But if lots of workers moved from A to B during the year, the region's overall rate can still go up, because more of the labor force now sits in the high-unemployment county. Rates of the parts don't fix the rate of the whole. We need something saying the mix didn't shift much.

choices.note: Other regions are irrelevant. The trend elsewhere tells us nothing about how Tarran's counties add up.
If anything, slightly worrying. It says the worst county improved the least, but it gives no information about the labor-force mix. It doesn't close the gap.

Tempting, since new jobs sound like lower unemployment. But we already know every county's rate fell. The question is whether those declines add up to a regional decline, and this says nothing about that.

CORRECT. If each county's share of the labor force barely changed, the weights in the regional average didn't shift. Every county's rate fell, so the weighted average fell too. This rules out the shift that could have broken the argument.
Irrelevant comparison. How fast Tarran's labor force grew compared with the country's has no bearing on whether the county declines add up to a regional one.

questions.stimulus: Broadcaster: Critics charge that our three-hour Saturday morning broadcast, which mixes cartoons with news and nature segments, exposes young children to too much distressing content. But a panel of child psychologists reviewed each of the broadcast's twelve segments separately and found that none contains too much distressing content for young children. So the critics' charge is unfounded.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the broadcaster's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that whatever is true of the broadcast as a whole must also be true of each of its segments
relies on the judgment of experts whose field has no bearing on the question of what content distresses children
overlooks the possibility that content acceptable in each of several portions can be excessive when the portions are combined
fails to consider that many of the people who regularly watch the broadcast are not young children
treats the failure to find evidence that a segment is distressing as proof that the segment is not distressing
questions.explanation: 'Too much' distressing content adds up: twelve segments that each stay under the limit can together exceed it over three hours. The broadcaster concludes that the whole lacks a property because no part has it, which (C) describes from the omission side, without the words 'part' or 'whole.' Most students pick (A), because it is the one answer that sounds like a part/whole flaw; but it runs the wrong direction, from the whole to its parts, and the broadcaster reasons from the segments to the broadcast.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics' charge that the broadcast exposes children to too much distressing content is unfounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A panel of child psychologists found that none of the twelve segments, taken separately, contains too much distressing content.

breakdown.analysis: Can twelve acceptable pieces add up to an unacceptable whole? Of course, when the property is an amount. One sad nature clip is fine; twelve segments each near the line, back to back for three hours, may not be. The broadcaster moves from 'no segment has too much' to 'the broadcast doesn't have too much.' That's a part-to-whole (composition) error. It's like saying each cookie is a small snack, so eating the whole box is a small snack. Prephrase: what's acceptable piece by piece can be too much in total. Most students pick (A), because it's labeled like part/whole. Check the direction.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the familiar part/whole language. But it's backward: it describes reasoning from the whole broadcast down to its segments. The broadcaster reasons from the segments up to the whole.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The orchestra is loud, so each violinist must be playing loudly.

choices.note: Child psychologists are exactly the right experts on what distresses young children. No mismatch.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous architect says this cartoon is fine for toddlers, so it is.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each segment passes on its own, but 'too much' is a total. Twelve passing segments can add up to an excessive three hours. That's the overlooked possibility.
Other viewers don't matter. The critics' charge and the panel's finding are both about young children.
The panel made a positive finding about each segment, not a failure to find anything. The problem is the step from segments to the whole.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has shown this segment upsets kids, so it doesn't.

questions.stimulus: A building firm wants its new model home to qualify for the state's top energy-efficiency rating. Every component the firm plans to install in the home, including the windows, the wall panels, the roofing, and the furnace, individually carries the state's top efficiency rating for its category. So once the home is built, it will qualify for the top rating.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Homes built entirely from top-rated components generally cost more to build than other homes of the same size and layout.
Some homes that the firm built in past years failed to qualify for the state's top energy-efficiency rating.
The state's top efficiency rating for windows is considerably easier for a manufacturer to obtain than its top rating for furnaces.
Few homebuyers in the state consider energy-efficiency ratings at all when deciding which of several homes to buy.
A finished home is rated mainly on how much heated air escapes at the joints where its windows, walls, and roof meet.
questions.explanation: The argument takes for granted that because every component is top rated, the whole home will be. (E) shows, without saying so outright, that the home's rating turns on joints between components, something no single component's rating can capture, so top-rated parts do not ensure a top-rated whole. Most students pick (B), because past failures seem to cast doubt on the firm; but nothing indicates those homes used top-rated components, so their failure says nothing about this plan.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new model home will qualify for the state's top efficiency rating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every component (windows, wall panels, roofing, furnace) carries the top rating for its category.

breakdown.analysis: Is a home just a pile of components? A home's efficiency depends on how the parts fit together, and no individual window test measures the gap between the window and the wall. The firm reasons from parts to whole. It's like assuming a band of great soloists will sound great together. To weaken: show the home's rating depends on something the component ratings miss. The correct answer never says 'parts' or 'whole'; you have to see that a joint belongs to no single component. Most students pick (B), because the firm's track record looks relevant. It isn't, unless those homes used top-rated parts too.

choices.note: Cost is a different dimension. The question is whether the home qualifies, not what it costs.
Tempting, because it suggests the firm has failed before. But we don't know those homes used top-rated components. Without that, their failure tells us nothing about this plan.
Ratings being easier for windows than furnaces doesn't matter; the firm has the top rating in every category regardless of how hard it was to get.
Buyer interest is irrelevant to whether the home qualifies.
CORRECT. If the home is rated mainly on leakage at the joints, and joints belong to no single component, then top-rated parts don't ensure a top-rated whole. The parts-to-whole leap fails.

questions.stimulus: The vineyards of the Morland Valley, taken together, produce more grapes per hectare than the vineyards of any other valley in the province. The Hessel vineyard is in the Morland Valley, and the Dunmore vineyard is in the neighboring Callan Valley, whose vineyards taken together yield less. Therefore, the Hessel vineyard produces more grapes per hectare than the Dunmore vineyard does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Kaur, a teller at the Elm Street branch, must process more transactions per hour than Lund, a teller at the Hill Road branch, since Elm Street's tellers as a group process more transactions per hour than the tellers at any other branch.

The Grafton school district spends more per student than any other district in the state, and its students score well on state exams. So Grafton's total spending on its schools must exceed that of every other district in the state.

Every physician at the Linden Clinic has more years of experience than any physician at the Rowe Clinic. Dr. Abe practices at Linden and Dr. Faro at Rowe. So Dr. Abe has more years of experience than Dr. Faro.

Each reporter at the Ledger writes more articles per week than any reporter at the Courier. Therefore, the Ledger's reporters, taken together, write more articles per week than the Courier's reporters do, and the Ledger is the more productive paper.

Most of the novels on this year's shortlist for the Arden Prize were written by first-time authors, as were most of last year's. Kemp's novel is on this year's shortlist. Therefore, Kemp is probably a first-time author.
questions.explanation: The stimulus infers that one member of a group outperforms one member of another group because the first group, taken as a whole, outperforms the second (division). (A) does the same, with its conclusion first. Most students pick (C), because it has the same cast (two groups, one named member of each, a head-to-head conclusion); but (C)'s premise is about every member of each clinic, so its conclusion follows validly. (D) is a part/whole flaw in the opposite direction, from members to the group.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Hessel vineyard produces more grapes per hectare than the Dunmore vineyard.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Morland Valley's vineyards, taken together, outyield every other valley's; Hessel is in Morland; Dunmore is in Callan, whose vineyards together yield less.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Group A as a whole beats group B as a whole; x is in A and y is in B; so x beats y.

breakdown.analysis: Does a strong team average mean every player on it beats every player on a weaker team? No. Morland could be full of high yielders with Hessel as its laggard, and Callan could have one superstar, Dunmore. The argument moves from a fact about groups to a fact about particular members: division. It's like saying any player from the champion team must be better than any player from the last-place team. Prephrase: group-level comparison used to rank two individuals. Most students pick (C), because its cast is identical. But (C) starts from every member of each clinic, so it's valid.

choices.note: CORRECT. Elm Street's tellers as a group are fastest, so one Elm Street teller must beat one Hill Road teller. Group-to-individual, just like Hessel and Dunmore, with the conclusion stated first.
Confuses a per-student figure with a total, a rate-versus-amount flaw. Grafton might be a small district. Not a group-to-member inference.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This café charges the most per coffee, so it must take in the most money.

choices.note: Tempting, because it has the same cast: two groups and one named member of each. But its premise covers every physician at each clinic, so Abe must beat Faro. Valid, so it can't match a flawed argument.
A part/whole flaw in the opposite direction: from each member to the group total (the Courier might have far more reporters).
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every player on our team is tall, so our team must be large.

choices.note: A cautious statistical inference ('probably') from 'most.' Reasonable, and not a group-to-member comparison between two individuals.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Lack of Evidence, Sampling, Analogy, Overreaching

questions.stimulus: Thirty years ago, recreational divers regularly reported seeing the comb jelly Lucerna vitrea in the waters off Cape Moray. Last spring, a research vessel spent six weeks towing fine-mesh plankton nets throughout those waters, and not one of its hundreds of hauls contained a specimen of Lucerna vitrea. Clearly, this species no longer lives off Cape Moray.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Lucerna vitrea is still commonly seen in coastal waters several hundred kilometers to the south of Cape Moray.
Average water temperatures off Cape Moray have risen noticeably over the past thirty years, a change that many jellies tolerate poorly.
Comb jellies such as Lucerna vitrea are so fragile that towed nets reduce them to unidentifiable fragments.
Most of the divers who reported seeing Lucerna vitrea thirty years ago were amateurs rather than trained marine biologists.
The plankton nets used off Cape Moray last spring captured large numbers of small crustaceans and fish larvae.
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the argument treats the nets' failure to turn up Lucerna vitrea as proof that the species is gone. C shows that towed nets would not yield a recognizable specimen even if the jelly were plentiful, so the empty hauls prove little. D is the tempting trap, but casting doubt on the old sightings does nothing to show the jelly is there now. A concerns a different location, and B, if anything, supports the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lucerna vitrea no longer lives off Cape Moray.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Divers reported it thirty years ago; six weeks of net hauls last spring caught no specimen.

breakdown.analysis: So the nets came up empty. Would the nets have caught this animal if it were there? If not, the empty hauls mean nothing. Not finding something is only evidence it's absent when your search could have found it. It's like checking for termites by looking for them in the mail: no termites in the mailbox doesn't mean the house is clean. We need an answer that says the nets were a bad way to detect this jelly.

choices.note: Wrong place. The conclusion is only about Cape Moray. Thriving hundreds of kilometers away says nothing about whether it lives off the cape.
Warmer water that jellies tolerate poorly gives a reason the species might have died off. If anything, this helps the conclusion.
CORRECT. If nets shred comb jellies beyond recognition, a net survey would come up empty whether or not the species is there. The silence of the hauls stops being evidence of absence.
Tempting. It attacks the old sightings, so it feels like it attacks the argument. But the conclusion is that the jelly isn't there now. Doubting that it was ever there doesn't show it's there today.
This shows the nets do catch small animals, which makes the survey look competent. That helps the argument, not hurts it.

questions.stimulus: Folklorist: Some scholars maintain that the legend of the drowned bell of Carrow was first told in inland farming villages and only later spread to the fishing towns on the coast. Yet in more than a century of collecting, folklorists have not recorded a single inland version of the legend that is older than the earliest coastal versions. So the legend must have originated in the coastal fishing towns.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the folklorist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats the absence of evidence for one account of the legend's origin as proof of a rival account
relies on the work of collectors without establishing that they are authorities on the legend's history
presumes that a legend told in two different kinds of communities must carry the same meaning in each
attempts to discredit the scholars' position by questioning their motives rather than the evidence they offer
takes for granted that a view held by most folklorists is more likely than not to be correct
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the folklorist moves from 'no old inland version has been recorded' to 'the legend began on the coast.' A names that leap; an inland oral tradition could be old without ever having been written down. B is the tempting trap because the argument does cite collectors, but it uses their records as data, not their opinions as authority.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Carrow bell legend originated in the coastal fishing towns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some scholars say it began inland; but no recorded inland version is older than the earliest coastal versions.

breakdown.analysis: So nobody wrote down an old inland version. Does that mean there wasn't one? Farming villages telling stories around the fire don't leave paper trails. The folklorist takes the scholars' lack of proof and treats it as proof of the opposite view. That's absence of evidence, a classic worth knowing. It's like saying: you can't prove you were home last night, so you must have been at the party. We need an answer that says lack of support for one view was treated as proof of the other.

choices.note: CORRECT. No recorded early inland version is a lack of evidence for the scholars' account. The folklorist treats it as establishing the coastal account, even though an old inland tradition might simply never have been written down.

Tempting, since the argument leans on a century of collecting. But it uses the collectors' records as data, not their opinions as authority. The problem isn't who collected; it's what the silence of the records can prove.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dr. Vance, a celebrated surgeon, says the bridge is structurally sound, so it must be.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument says nothing about what the legend means in each place.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The bell legend is told inland and on the coast, so it must symbolize the same loss in both.

choices.note: The folklorist never mentions the scholars' motives. No personal attack here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The scholars only say it began inland because they are from inland families, so they're wrong.

choices.note: The argument never appeals to what most folklorists believe. It appeals to what they have recorded.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most folklorists think the legend is coastal, so it probably is.

questions.stimulus: Mining consultant: For decades, prospectors who have worked the hills above Dunmere have claimed that the hills contain a rich vein of silver. But not one of these prospectors has ever produced an assay report confirming that claim. So there is no rich vein of silver in the hills above Dunmere.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Prospectors have long claimed that the hills above Dunmere hold a rich vein of silver. But a state survey of those hills, thorough enough to have detected any such vein, found none. So there is no rich vein of silver there.
Every geologist who has studied the Kelso basin believes it holds natural gas. Since these geologists are the leading experts on the region, the basin must hold natural gas.
Three of the wells recently drilled near the village of Ashby struck fresh water at a shallow depth. So nearly every well drilled anywhere in the county will strike fresh water.
If a cave is home to a bat colony, its floor will be covered with guano. The floor of Orrin Cave is covered with guano. So Orrin Cave is home to a bat colony.
A local legend says the poet Ilse Varn wrote her last poems at the Crane Inn. But no letter or diary from her time places her there. So she did not write them at the inn.
questions.explanation: The consultant concludes that a claim is false merely because no one has confirmed it. (E) has the same shape in a different setting: a legend, no confirming record, so the legend is false. Most students pick (A), because it repeats the stimulus's prospectors, hills and silver almost word for word; but (A) relies on a survey thorough enough to have found the vein, which is real evidence of absence, so (A) is sound and cannot match a flawed argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: There is no rich vein of silver in the hills above Dunmere.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Prospectors have claimed for decades that there is, but none has produced an assay confirming it.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: People claim X; no one has confirmed X; so X is false.

breakdown.analysis: No one has proven the vein exists. Does that prove it doesn't? No. Maybe no prospector could afford an assay. Lack of proof for a claim isn't proof against it. That's the absence-of-evidence flaw; know it. It's like saying your keys can't be in the house because you haven't found them yet. Prephrase: a claim rejected only because it was never confirmed. Now the key distinction: evidence of absence is different. A search that would have found the thing, and didn't, is real evidence. Most students pick (A), because it's the stimulus's own story. But (A)'s survey would have found the vein, so its reasoning is fine.

choices.note: Tempting: same hills, same silver, same conclusion. But here a survey thorough enough to detect any vein found none. That's evidence the vein isn't there, not mere lack of proof that it is. Sound reasoning can't match a flawed argument.
An appeal to expert consensus. Experts can be wrong, but this concludes something is true because authorities believe it, not false because it's unconfirmed.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All the critics love this film, so it must be a masterpiece.

choices.note: A hasty generalization from three wells to the whole county. Different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My two cousins love jazz, so most people do.

choices.note: Reverses a conditional: bats → guano; guano, so bats. Different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained.

choices.note: CORRECT. A claim (the legend) has no confirming record, so it's declared false. Same move: lack of confirmation treated as disproof, in a new setting.

questions.stimulus: Epidemiologists have determined that a recent outbreak of intestinal illness in the town of Pellam was caused by the bacterium Kesselia aquatilis. Two weeks after the first cases were reported, health officials collected water samples from each of the twelve wells that supply the town. None of the samples contained Kesselia aquatilis. The officials concluded that the outbreak did not result from contamination of the town's wells.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the officials' argument depends?
choices: None of the Pellam residents who drink only bottled water rather than well water became ill during the outbreak.
Well contamination heavy enough to cause the outbreak would still have been detectable two weeks after the first cases.
The water samples were tested using the most sensitive method now available for detecting Kesselia aquatilis in water.
Kesselia aquatilis cannot be passed directly from one person to another through ordinary household contact.
No earlier outbreak of intestinal illness in Pellam has ever been traced to the town's wells.
questions.explanation: Clean samples taken two weeks after the first cases count as evidence of clean wells only if contamination that caused the outbreak would still have been there to find. (B) states that requirement without using the word 'evidence.' Most students pick (C), because test quality matters; but it is the right worry at the wrong strength: the argument needs an adequate test, not the most sensitive one available, so negating (C) does no harm.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The outbreak did not result from contamination of the town's wells.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kesselia aquatilis caused the outbreak; two weeks after the first cases, samples from all twelve wells showed no Kesselia aquatilis.

breakdown.analysis: Two weeks later. What if the bacteria were in a well, caused the outbreak, and then washed out or died off?
