Then clean samples tell you nothing about the wells back when people got sick. The officials treat 'not found now' as 'wasn't there then.' That's absence of evidence doing the work of evidence of absence. It's like checking a room for a burglar a week after the break-in and concluding no one broke in. Prephrase: contamination that caused the outbreak would still have shown up two weeks later. Most students pick (C), because a weak test is a familiar worry. But 'the most sensitive method available' is far more than the argument needs.

choices.note: Not required. Negate it: some bottled-water drinkers got sick. That actually points away from the wells, so it doesn't hurt the officials at all.
choices.negation: At least one Pellam resident who drinks only bottled water rather than well water became ill during the outbreak.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: well contamination heavy enough to cause the outbreak could have become undetectable within two weeks. Then the clean samples prove nothing about the wells, and the conclusion has no support.
choices.negation: Well contamination heavy enough to cause the outbreak might not have been detectable two weeks after the first cases.

choices.note: Tempting, because a weak test would undercut clean results. But too strong: the officials need an adequate test, not the best one in existence. Negate it (a more sensitive method exists) and the samples can still be reliable.
choices.negation: The water samples were not tested using the most sensitive method now available for detecting Kesselia aquatilis in water.

choices.note: Person-to-person spread is a different route, and the argument doesn't need to rule it out to conclude the wells weren't the source. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Kesselia aquatilis can be passed directly from one person to another through ordinary household contact.

choices.note: History is irrelevant. Even if earlier outbreaks came from the wells, this one might not have. Negating it doesn't touch the reasoning.
choices.negation: At least one earlier outbreak of intestinal illness in Pellam has been traced to the town's wells.

questions.stimulus: Traffic engineer: Residents of Holloway Street blame the bicycle lane added last year for the rise in rear-end collisions there since then. But the police report on every one of those collisions lists the factors that contributed to the crash, such as following too closely, driver distraction, or wet pavement, and not one report mentions the bicycle lane. So the lane did not contribute to the rise.
questions.stem: The traffic engineer's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: rejects the residents' claim solely on the grounds that the residents lack expertise in traffic safety
takes for granted that the fact that two events occurred together shows that one caused the other
fails to consider that collisions on Holloway Street might have increased even if the bicycle lane had not been added
overlooks the possibility that a factor the reports do mention was itself brought about in part by the bicycle lane
concludes that the bicycle lane is safe for cyclists from evidence concerning only collisions between motor vehicles
questions.explanation: The reports' silence about the lane is treated as proof that the lane played no role. But the lane could act through the very factors the reports list: a narrowed travel lane, for instance, can lead drivers to follow more closely. (D) points to this route without ever saying 'absence of evidence.' Most students pick (B), because correlation-to-causation is the textbook flaw in collision stories; but that is the residents' reasoning, and the engineer denies a causal link rather than inferring one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bicycle lane did not contribute to the rise in rear-end collisions.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every collision report lists contributing factors (following too closely, distraction, wet pavement); none mentions the bicycle lane.

breakdown.analysis: Would a crash report ever say 'bicycle lane'? Reports list what the drivers did: followed too closely, looked at a phone. But why were they following so closely? Maybe because the lane squeezed traffic into a narrower space. The lane could be behind a factor the reports DO list. So the reports' silence about the lane proves nothing. That's an absence-of-evidence flaw in disguise. It's like concluding a heat wave didn't cause any deaths because the death certificates say 'heart attack.' Prephrase: the lane could have worked through the listed factors. Most students pick (B), the classic causal flaw. But the engineer is denying a cause, not inferring one from a correlation.

choices.note: The engineer never mentions the residents' expertise. The rebuttal rests on the police reports.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The residents aren't traffic engineers, so their claim about the lane is wrong.

choices.note: Tempting, because a before-and-after collision story usually hides a correlation flaw. But that's the residents' reasoning. The engineer concludes the lane did NOT cause anything, so he isn't inferring cause from co-occurrence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions rose after the lane was added, so the lane caused them.

choices.note: This would help the engineer, not hurt him: if collisions would have risen anyway, that's a reason to doubt the lane mattered. Not a flaw in his reasoning.

CORRECT. The reports list factors like following too closely. If the lane helped produce those behaviors, it contributed even though no report names it. The engineer overlooks this, treating the reports' silence as proof.
The engineer says nothing about cyclists' safety. The conclusion is only about rear-end collisions between vehicles.

questions.stimulus: Of the 400 cats examined during routine annual checkups at the Corvale Animal Clinic last year, 35 percent were overweight. The clinic is the largest in Corvale, and its clients come from every neighborhood in the city, rich and poor alike. So roughly a third of all the pet cats in Corvale are overweight.
questions.stem: The argument is flawed in that it
choices: takes for granted that being overweight is harmful to the long-term health of a pet cat
fails to consider that cats taken for annual checkups may differ in weight from other pet cats
confuses the percentage of examined cats that were overweight with the number of overweight cats in Corvale
relies on the clinic's size as evidence of the competence of the veterinarians who work there
draws a conclusion about the clinic's future clients from data about the clients it served last year
questions.explanation: Sampling: the sample is cats brought in for routine annual checkups, but the conclusion covers all pet cats in Corvale. B points out that cats whose owners schedule yearly checkups may differ from the rest, and the clinic's citywide reach does nothing to fix that. C is the tempting trap because there are numbers, but the argument concludes about a proportion, not a count.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Roughly a third of all pet cats in Corvale are overweight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 35% of the 400 cats examined at the clinic's annual checkups were overweight; the clinic is the city's largest and draws from every neighborhood.

breakdown.analysis: Who brings a cat in for an annual checkup? Owners who are attentive enough to schedule one. Their cats could be fed differently, be older, or be indoor cats. Coverage of every neighborhood fixes geography, not the type of owner. It's like surveying gym members about exercise and calling the result 'the city's habits.' We need an answer that says the checkup cats may not represent all pet cats.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about how many cats are overweight, not whether that's harmful.
CORRECT. The sample is cats whose owners bring them in for checkups. They may differ in weight from cats who never see a vet, so the 35% may not hold for all pet cats.
Tempting, because there are percentages. But the conclusion is a proportion ('roughly a third'), not a count. No confusion of percent and number here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: 35% of cats in Corvale are overweight but only 10% in Linden, so Corvale has more overweight cats.

choices.note: The clinic's size is used to suggest a broad sample, not to vouch for its vets' skill.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ours is the biggest clinic in town, so our vets must be the best.

choices.note: The conclusion is about all pet cats in Corvale now, not the clinic's future clients. The argument never makes a prediction about who will visit.

questions.stimulus: The Larkfield Folk Dance Society mailed a questionnaire to all 400 of its members asking whether they would attend a proposed monthly evening dance. Of the 120 members who returned the questionnaire, 85 said that they would attend. On the basis of these results, the society's director concluded that a majority of the society's members would attend the monthly dance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?
choices: Most residents of Larkfield who do not belong to the society have never attended a folk dance of any kind.
The questionnaire also asked members which evening of the week they would prefer for the proposed dance.
The members who returned the questionnaire included both long-standing members and members who had joined within the past year.
Members who did not return the questionnaire attend the society's events about as often as those who returned it.
Several of the members who said they would attend added that they would come only if the dance ended by ten o'clock.
questions.explanation: Sampling: only 120 of 400 members answered, and people who bother to return a questionnaire may be the keenest. D strengthens by showing the non-respondents are about as engaged as the respondents, so the 85-of-120 figure is more likely to hold for the whole membership. C is the tempting trap; mixing old and new members shows variety on one dimension but says nothing about whether the respondents were unusually eager.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A majority of the society's 400 members would attend the monthly dance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 120 members returned the questionnaire, and 85 of them said they'd attend.

breakdown.analysis: Who sends back a questionnaire about a dance? The people who love dances. The 280 who didn't answer might be the ones who'd stay home. That's a self-selected sample. We need an answer that says the non-responders look like the responders in the way that matters: their interest in coming to events.

choices.note: Wrong group. Non-members' habits don't tell us what members will do.
Irrelevant. What else the questionnaire asked doesn't make the answers more representative.
Tempting. It sounds like the respondents were a good mix. But a mix of old and new members doesn't show they weren't the most enthusiastic ones. It fixes a dimension that doesn't matter.
CORRECT. The worry is that responders are keener than non-responders. If non-responders attend events just as often, the sample's yes rate is more likely to reflect the whole membership.
This casts doubt on some of the 85 yeses. If anything, it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Last month Harwick Bank interviewed every small-business owner who had received a loan from the bank during the past year, and nearly all of them described the bank's application process as quick and easy. Clearly, then, nearly all small-business owners who apply for a loan at Harwick Bank find the application process quick and easy.
questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
choices: Each of the forty questions on the Ardmore aptitude exam can, by itself, be answered in under a minute. So the Ardmore exam as a whole can be completed in under a minute.

A random sample of all the people who applied for a fishing license this year found that nearly all of them considered the application form clear. So nearly all applicants for fishing licenses find the form clear.
Nearly all of the hikers who signed the logbook at the summit of Mount Ostrel this season described the trail as manageable. So nearly all hikers who attempt the trail find it manageable.
Gardeners who spread Verda mulch around their flower beds this spring reported fewer weeds than gardeners who did not. So spreading Verda mulch causes gardens to have fewer weeds.
No customer of Ravel Hardware has ever filed a written complaint about the store's return policy. So every one of Ravel Hardware's customers is satisfied with that policy.
questions.explanation: The bank hears only from applicants who succeeded (got a loan) and generalizes to everyone who applies, including those who gave up or were rejected. (C) does the same: it hears only from hikers who reached the summit and generalizes to everyone who attempts the trail. Most students pick (B), because it matches the topic and nearly the wording; but its random sample of all applicants is representative, so its reasoning is sound and cannot match a flawed argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly all small-business owners who apply to Harwick find the application process quick and easy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly all owners who received loans in the past year said so.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Surveyed only those who succeeded at X; concluded about everyone who attempts X.

breakdown.analysis: Who did they ask? Only people who got loans. What about owners who gave up halfway through the paperwork, or got rejected? They're exactly the people likely to call the process hard. This is a survivor-only sample. Find the answer that surveys only the successful and concludes about everyone who tried. Most students pick (B), because it's the near-copy: applications, 'nearly all,' 'find it clear.' But (B) samples ALL applicants at random, which is exactly what the bank failed to do.

choices.note: Different flaw: part to whole. Each question is quick, so the whole exam is quick.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every brick in the wall is light, so the wall is light.

choices.note: Tempting. Same topic (applications) and nearly the same wording. But this sample is random and drawn from ALL applicants, so it's representative. Its reasoning is fine. A sound argument can't match a flawed one.

CORRECT. Only hikers who reached the top signed the logbook. Hikers who turned back, the ones most likely to find it hard, were never heard from. Same survivor-only sample as the bank's survey of owners who got loans.
Different flaw: correlation treated as causation. Mulch users have fewer weeds, so mulch causes it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Students who eat breakfast get better grades, so breakfast raises grades.

choices.note: Different flaw: treating the absence of complaints as proof of satisfaction. It's not a sample at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has told me my cooking is bad, so everyone loves it.

questions.stimulus: Last year the city of Brennock installed speed humps along Alder Lane, a residential street, as a trial. Within two months, average vehicle speeds on Alder Lane had fallen by nearly a third. The city's traffic engineer therefore argues that installing speed humps on Brennock's other residential streets would reduce average speeds on those streets by a similar proportion.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the traffic engineer's argument?
choices: Most of Brennock's residential streets, unlike Alder Lane, are short and winding, and drivers on them already travel well below the speed limit.
After the speed humps were installed, some drivers who had regularly used Alder Lane began using nearby streets instead.
Speed humps can slightly delay fire trucks and ambulances responding to emergencies on residential streets, a concern raised by city officials.
Average speeds on Alder Lane fell further during the second month of the trial than they did during the first.
Residents of several other streets in Brennock have petitioned the city to install speed humps on their streets.
questions.explanation: The engineer generalizes from one trial street to all residential streets. (A) shows Alder Lane was atypical: the city's other streets are already slow, so there is far less speed for humps to cut there, and a one-third drop is unlikely. Most students pick (B), because displaced traffic sounds like a hidden cost of the trial; but it concerns where drivers go, not how much humps slow the drivers who use a street.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Speed humps on Brennock's other residential streets would cut average speeds by a similar proportion.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On Alder Lane, a trial street, average speeds fell by nearly a third within two months of installing humps.

breakdown.analysis: One street. Is Alder Lane typical? If drivers raced down it, humps had a lot of speed to take away. On streets where people already crawl, there's little left to cut. The engineer treats a sample of one as representative of all residential streets. It's like testing a diet on the heaviest person in town and promising everyone the same weight loss. To weaken: show Alder Lane differs from the other streets in a way that affects the result. Notice the right answer never mentions the trial. Most students pick (B), because rerouted drivers sound like a flaw in the trial. But the claim is about speeds on streets with humps.

choices.note: CORRECT. Alder Lane is atypical: the other streets are short, winding and already slow. Humps there have little speed to remove, so 'a similar proportion' is unlikely. The sample of one doesn't represent the population.
Tempting, because it sounds like the trial had a side effect. But traffic moving elsewhere is about volume, not about how much humps slow drivers on the streets that get them.
A cost of the plan, not a reason to doubt the speed prediction. Wrong dimension.
This makes the Alder Lane effect look stronger and more durable. If anything it helps the engineer.
Residents' wishes don't show whether the humps would cut speeds there.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, borrowers at Fenwick Credit who completed the lender's optional six-week budgeting course defaulted on their loans at a rate of 3 percent, compared with 8 percent among Fenwick's other borrowers. Fenwick's managers therefore plan to require every new borrower to complete the course, expecting that this requirement will bring the default rate among new borrowers down to about 3 percent.
questions.stem: The reasoning behind the managers' expectation is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats a reduction in the rate at which borrowers default as though it guaranteed a reduction in the total number of defaults
overlooks the possibility that running the course for every borrower would cost more than fewer defaults would save
presumes that what is true of a group of borrowers taken as a whole must be true of each borrower in that group
takes for granted that the default rate among Fenwick's borrowers is higher than the default rate at other lenders
treats the outcome for those who volunteered for something as predictive of the outcome for those compelled to do it
questions.explanation: The 3 percent figure comes from borrowers who chose a budgeting course, and volunteers are likely more careful with money to begin with. (E) says, abstractly, that the managers project this self-selected group's results onto borrowers who will be compelled to take part. Most students pick (A), because the stimulus is full of rates and rate-versus-number is a familiar trap; but the managers' expectation concerns a rate throughout, so no rate is confused with a number.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring the course for every new borrower will bring the new-borrower default rate down to about 3%.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Over five years, borrowers who took the optional course defaulted at 3%, versus 8% for other borrowers.

breakdown.analysis: Who signs up for an optional budgeting course? Borrowers who already care about their finances. They might default at 3% with or without the course. Force everyone to take it, and you add the people who'd never have chosen it, who may default just as much as before. The volunteers are a self-selected sample. It's like noting that people who voluntarily join a running club are fit, and then expecting a mandatory running club to make everyone that fit. We need an answer that says results from volunteers won't carry over to people who are made to join. Most students pick (A), because rates and numbers are both in the air. But the managers predict a default RATE from a default RATE; nothing is confused.

choices.note: Tempting, since there are rates everywhere. But the managers expect a lower RATE, and their evidence is about rates. Nothing is confused with a number of borrowers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our default rate fell from 8% to 3%, so we must have fewer defaults this year, even though we doubled our lending.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The managers only predict a lower default rate. Whether the course pays for itself is a different question.
Different flaw: division. The managers predict a group rate, not what each borrower will do.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Course graduates default at 3%, so Ms. Ruiz, a graduate, has a 3% chance of defaulting no matter what.

choices.note: The argument never compares Fenwick with other lenders. Nothing here needs that assumption.

CORRECT. The 3% comes from borrowers who chose the course. The plan applies it to borrowers who are forced to take it. Volunteers may simply be more careful with money, so their results don't predict the mandatory group's.

questions.stimulus: Apartment manager: Our building's lease forbids tenants to keep dogs, because barking dogs disturb the neighbors. Ferrets, like dogs, are carnivorous mammals, and many people in apartments like ours keep them as household pets. So, for the sake of consistency, the lease should also forbid tenants to keep ferrets.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the apartment manager's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that every dog kept by a tenant would bark often enough to disturb the neighbors
fails to consider that some tenants may wish to keep both a dog and a ferret in the same apartment
treats the popularity of a kind of pet as evidence that it is suitable for apartment living
treats as relevant some similarities between dogs and ferrets that have no bearing on why dogs are banned
draws a conclusion about all ferrets from the observed behavior of only a few ferrets in the building
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: dogs are banned because they bark, but the manager extends the ban to ferrets on the basis of traits (being carnivorous mammals and popular pets) that have nothing to do with barking. D names this. A is the tempting trap, but the rule's rationale is a premise the manager accepts; the flaw is in the step from dogs to ferrets.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lease should also forbid ferrets.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dogs are banned because barking disturbs neighbors; ferrets, like dogs, are carnivorous mammals and popular pets.

breakdown.analysis: Why are dogs banned? Barking. Do ferrets bark? The manager never says. The similarities offered, carnivorous mammal and popular pet, have nothing to do with noise. An analogy only works if the cases share the feature that matters. It's like saying: we ban drums in the building because they're loud, and guitars, like drums, are musical instruments, so we should ban guitars. We need an answer that says the similarities are irrelevant to the reason for the rule.

choices.note: Tempting. The rule's reason does overgeneralize about dogs. But that's a premise the manager accepts, not the step being criticized. The flaw is in jumping from dogs to ferrets.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Some dogs bark at night, so every dog in the building would keep the neighbors awake.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether a tenant wants both pets has nothing to do with whether the comparison holds.
The manager mentions that ferrets are popular, but doesn't argue they're suitable because they're popular. The conclusion is that they should be banned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Lots of people keep pet pythons, so pythons are fine for apartments.

choices.note: CORRECT. The rule exists because dogs bark. Being a carnivorous mammal or a popular pet has nothing to do with barking, so the shared traits don't support the same rule.
There's no sample of ferrets here at all. The argument is about the category, not observed ferrets.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The two ferrets I've met bit me, so all ferrets bite.

questions.stimulus: After high-capacity ventilation fans were installed in the Garrow mine, airborne dust levels there fell by 40 percent. The mining company's planned Teller mine will extract the same kind of ore from rock at a similar depth. So installing the same fans at the Teller mine will reduce dust levels there by a comparable amount.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Workers at the Teller mine will be required to wear respirators that filter out most airborne dust.
Unlike Garrow's long, straight tunnels, the Teller mine will have many short, branching galleries in which air circulates poorly.
Operating the high-capacity fans costs considerably more each year than operating the older fans they replaced at the Garrow mine did.
Several other mines in the region that installed the same fans also saw large reductions in their dust levels.
Ore from the Garrow mine is sold to the same smelters that are expected to buy ore from the Teller mine.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the argument takes for granted that Teller will respond like Garrow because the two mines share ore type and depth. B shows a difference that bears directly on how fans work: air does not circulate well through Teller's branching layout. A is the tempting trap; respirators protect workers, but they do nothing to the dust levels in the air, which is what the conclusion is about.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The same fans will cut dust levels at the Teller mine by about 40%.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The fans cut dust 40% at Garrow; Teller will mine the same ore at a similar depth.

breakdown.analysis: Same ore, same depth. Fine, but what makes a fan work? Moving air through the mine. If the two mines are shaped differently, the fans might not move air the same way. The analogy rests on similarities that may not be the ones that matter. We need a relevant difference: something about Teller that would make the fans less effective.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's about dust and worker health. But respirators filter what workers breathe; they don't change how much dust is in the air. The conclusion is about dust levels in the mine.

CORRECT. Fans reduce dust by moving air. If air circulates poorly through Teller's branching galleries, the fans won't clear dust the way they did in Garrow's straight tunnels. That's a relevant difference.
Wrong dimension. Cost doesn't affect how much dust the fans remove. The conclusion is about effectiveness.
More mines with good results. This strengthens the case for the fans.
Irrelevant. Who buys the ore has nothing to do with how air moves underground.

questions.stimulus: Dance company director: Two years ago the Varga Ballet stopped performing on Monday evenings, and its average ticket sales per performance rose substantially. Our company, like the Varga Ballet, performs in a city of about half a million people and stages mostly classical works. So we too should stop performing on Monday evenings, in order to increase our ticket sales per performance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: When Hollis Bakery stopped opening on Mondays, its weekly profits rose. Our café, like Hollis, is on Main Street and is known for its pastries. So we should stop opening on Mondays to raise our weekly profits.

When Hollis Bakery stopped opening on Mondays, its weekly profits rose, because its Monday sales never covered its Monday staffing costs. Our café's Monday sales have never covered its Monday staffing costs either. So we should stop opening on Mondays to raise our weekly profits.
Three cafés on Main Street raised their prices last year and kept all of their regular customers. So any café in town could raise its prices by a similar amount without losing customers.

Every café on Main Street whose profits rose last year had stopped opening on Mondays. Hollis Bakery, a café on Main Street, stopped opening on Mondays last year. So Hollis Bakery's profits must have risen.
Most of the shops on Main Street close on Mondays. So our café should close on Mondays as well, since following the practice of most of our neighbors is the surest way to raise our profits.
questions.explanation: The director copies the Varga Ballet's policy on the strength of similarities (city size, repertoire) not shown to matter to Monday attendance. (A) copies Hollis Bakery's policy on the strength of shared location and pastries, which likewise are not shown to bear on Monday profits. Most students pick (B), because it uses the same policy and the same structure; but (B) cites the very similarity that explains the result, so its analogy is sound.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: We should stop performing on Mondays to raise ticket sales per performance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Varga stopped Monday shows and its per-show sales rose; we, like Varga, are in a city of ~500,000 and stage mostly classical works.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Business X did A and got result R; we share some features with X (not shown to matter); so we should do A to get R.

breakdown.analysis: Why did Varga's sales per show rise? Maybe their Monday crowds were tiny, maybe they moved those patrons to weekends. The director doesn't know. City size and classical repertoire aren't shown to be what made the change work. It's like copying your neighbor's diet because you both drive Hondas. Find the argument that copies a policy based on similarities that aren't connected to why the policy worked. Most students pick (B), because it's the same policy with the same shape. But (B) names the reason the policy worked and shows the café shares it. That's a good analogy, so it can't match a flawed one.

choices.note: CORRECT. Hollis closed Mondays and profits rose. Our café shares a street and a reputation for pastries, neither shown to matter to Monday business. So we should copy them. Same weak analogy as the director's.

Tempting. Same policy, same structure. But this one cites the actual reason the policy worked (Monday sales didn't cover Monday costs) and shows the café shares it. That's a good analogy, not a flawed one.
Different flaw: hasty generalization from three cafés to every café in town.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Two of my friends liked the new restaurant, so everyone will like it.

choices.note: Different flaw: confusing necessary and sufficient. Closing Mondays is required for the profit rise, not a guarantee of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Everyone who passed studied; Lee studied; so Lee passed.

choices.note: Different flaw: appeal to popularity. Most neighbors do it, so we should. No comparison to one business's results.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most people in town shop at Delmar's, so it must have the best prices.

questions.stimulus: Twenty years ago a warm current began shifting northward along the coast of the Brisa Gulf, and within a decade the gulf's kelp forests had largely collapsed. A warm current is now shifting northward in the same way along the Corran coast. So the kelp forests off the Corran coast will probably collapse within the next decade or so.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The shift of the warm current in the Brisa Gulf had no effects on marine life there other than the collapse of the kelp forests.
The warm current off the Corran coast is shifting northward at exactly the same rate as the current in the Brisa Gulf did.
No kelp forest has ever collapsed in a region where no warm current was shifting northward.
The kelp forests off the Corran coast cover a larger area than the kelp forests of the Brisa Gulf did.
The kelp forests off the Corran coast are not substantially more tolerant of warm water than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests were.
questions.explanation: The prediction for Corran rests on Corran's being like the Brisa Gulf in the respects that matter. (E) rules out one relevant difference: if Corran's kelp were far more heat tolerant, the Brisa outcome would be a poor guide. Most students pick (B), because the current's rate seems crucial; but 'exactly the same rate' is far stronger than the argument needs: a similar shift would do, so negating (B) leaves the argument intact.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corran's kelp forests will probably collapse within a decade or so.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A warm current's northward shift in the Brisa Gulf was followed by kelp collapse; a similar shift is happening along the Corran coast.

breakdown.analysis: Same kind of current shift, so the same result? Only if the kelp is comparable. What if Corran's kelp handles warm water far better than Brisa's did? Then the comparison falls apart. The argument needs the two cases to be alike in the way that matters. Prephrase: Corran's kelp is not much hardier against warm water than Brisa's was. Note the modest wording: the assumption is 'not substantially more tolerant,' not 'identical.' Most students pick (B), because the current is the cause in the story. But it's the right idea at the wrong strength: 'exactly the same rate' isn't needed when a similar shift would do.

choices.note: Not required. The current could have done other things to Brisa's marine life too. Negate it and the kelp prediction is untouched.
choices.negation: The shift of the warm current in the Brisa Gulf had at least one effect on marine life there other than the kelp collapse.

choices.note: Tempting, because the rate of change seems relevant. But 'exactly the same' is too strong. Negated, the rates differ slightly, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: The warm current off the Corran coast is not shifting at exactly the same rate as the Brisa Gulf current did.

choices.note: Too strong and off point. Kelp could collapse for other reasons elsewhere without hurting this prediction. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one kelp forest has collapsed in a region where no warm current was shifting northward.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Size isn't tied to vulnerability here. Negate it (Corran's are not larger) and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The kelp forests off the Corran coast do not cover a larger area than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests did.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Corran's kelp is substantially more tolerant of warm water. Then the Brisa outcome tells us little about Corran, and the prediction loses its support.
choices.negation: The kelp forests off the Corran coast are substantially more tolerant of warm water than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests were.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Critics charge that short-term cash-advance loans are exploitative, noting that their fees amount to annual interest rates of several hundred percent. But a $150-a-night hotel room would cost nearly $55,000 if rented for a year, and no one judges a nightly rate by that figure, since hotel rooms are meant for short stays. Likewise, cash advances are meant to be repaid within a few weeks. So annualized interest rates are a misleading measure of what these loans cost.
questions.stem: The economist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that the nightly rates charged by hotels are fair to the guests who pay them
attempts to discredit the critics' position by questioning their motives for advancing it rather than their evidence
overlooks the possibility that one of the arrangements compared is often kept far longer than intended
treats a claim about cash-advance loans in general as though it held for each individual loan
concludes that the loans are not exploitative merely because one argument that they are has been shown to be flawed
questions.explanation: The hotel comparison works only if borrowers, like hotel guests, actually use the arrangement briefly. (C) points out, without naming either, that what something is meant for is not how long it is in fact used: if borrowers routinely roll advances over for months, annualized rates are not misleading. Most students pick (E), because 'one bad argument refuted, so the opposite is true' fits many rebuttals; but the economist never concludes the loans aren't exploitative, only that one measure of their cost is misleading.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Annualized interest rates are a misleading measure of what cash advances cost borrowers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A $150/night hotel room costs ~$55,000 a year, but we don't judge hotels that way because rooms are meant for short stays; cash advances are likewise meant to be repaid within weeks.

breakdown.analysis: Hotel guests really do leave after a few nights. Do borrowers really repay in a few weeks? The economist only says the loans are MEANT to be repaid quickly. If many borrowers keep rolling the loan over for months, the annual rate is exactly what they pay, and the hotel comparison breaks down. That's a flawed analogy: the cases differ on the one feature the argument relies on, how long people actually stay in. It's like saying a gym's daily pass is cheap because it's 'meant for one visit,' when most buyers come every day. We need an answer that says the loans may in practice last much longer than intended. Most students pick (E), because it's the standard rebuttal flaw. Read the conclusion: it's only that annualized rates mislead, not that the loans are fair.

choices.note: Tempting, since the hotel is the economist's example. But the point isn't that hotel prices are fair; it's that annualizing a short-term price is misleading. The argument works even if hotels overcharge.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Hotels charge $150 a night, so that must be a fair price for a room.

choices.note: The economist never mentions the critics' motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics run competing banks, so their complaint about cash advances can be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. Cash advances are meant to last weeks, but borrowers may often roll them over for months. Unlike a hotel stay, the 'short-term' use may not be real, and then the annual rate is a fair measure.
Different flaw: division. The economist talks about the loans as a type and doesn't infer anything about each individual loan.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Cash advances on average are repaid in three weeks, so Ms. Ono's will be repaid in three weeks.

choices.note: Tempting, since this flaw fits a lot of rebuttals. But read the conclusion: annualized rates are misleading. The economist never says the loans aren't exploitative.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics' math is wrong, so the loans are not exploitative.

questions.stimulus: Halden fever, a mosquito-borne illness, can be prevented in part by the use of bed nets and insect repellent. In a two-year trial, children randomly assigned to receive a new Halden fever vaccine contracted the disease at one-twentieth the rate of children randomly assigned to receive a placebo. A public health official concluded from these results that vaccination is the most effective way to protect children from Halden fever.
questions.stem: The public health official's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: infers that a measure is the best option from evidence that it is better than doing nothing
confuses the rate at which young children contracted Halden fever with the number of children who contracted it
presumes, without providing justification, that the vaccine has no harmful side effects when it is given to young children
relies on a comparison between groups of children who were not assigned to those two groups at random
takes for granted that an illness that few children contract cannot be a serious threat to children's health
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the trial compares the vaccine only with a placebo, so it shows the vaccine is effective, not that it is the most effective option. A names the jump from 'better than nothing' to 'best'; bed nets and repellent were never tested. B is the tempting trap because of the rates, but the official draws no conclusion about numbers of cases.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vaccination is the most effective way to protect children from Halden fever.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a randomized trial, vaccinated children got the disease at 1/20 the rate of placebo children; bed nets and repellent also prevent it.

breakdown.analysis: The vaccine beat a placebo. A placebo is nothing. So the vaccine beats nothing. How does it compare with bed nets or repellent? The trial never tested them. Watch the jump from 'works' to 'works best.' It's like saying a bike is the fastest way to get to work because it beats walking. We need an answer that says the evidence compares the vaccine only with no protection.

choices.note: CORRECT. The trial shows the vaccine is far better than a placebo, that is, than doing nothing. It says nothing about bed nets or repellent, so 'most effective' isn't supported.
Tempting, since numbers are flying. But the official never draws a conclusion about how many children got sick, only about which method is most effective.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The disease rate fell by half, so half as many children got sick, even though the population tripled.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Side effects matter to whether to vaccinate, but the conclusion is only about effectiveness.
Just false: the stimulus says both groups were randomly assigned. This answer is for readers who skim.
The official says nothing about how serious the illness is.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Few kids catch it, so it can't be dangerous.

questions.stimulus: Mining official: Ten years ago the Ostrava mining district adopted strict rules requiring water sprays and dust masks in all underground work. Since then, the rate at which the district's miners develop lung disease has fallen by half. Thanks to these rules, then, the district's miners now face only a low risk of lung disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the mining official's argument depends?
choices: The decline in the rate of lung disease among the district's miners was not due to any factor other than the dust rules.
Miners in districts that have not adopted similar rules develop lung disease at a higher rate than the district's miners now do.
No miner in the district who has fully complied with the dust rules over the past ten years has developed lung disease.
Dust is the only cause of lung disease among the miners who work underground in the Ostrava district.
The district's former rate of lung disease was not so high that half that rate would still be high.
questions.explanation: Scope shift from a relative claim (the rate fell by half) to an absolute one (the risk is now low). Halving a very high rate can still leave a high rate, so the argument requires E. A is the tempting trap, but it is too strong: the rules need only to have produced the decline, not to be its sole cause, for the official's 'thanks to these rules' to stand.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Thanks to the dust rules, the district's miners now face only a low risk of lung disease.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the rules were adopted ten years ago, the lung-disease rate has fallen by half.

breakdown.analysis: Cut in half. Is half low? If 60% of miners used to get lung disease, now it's 30%, and that's still terrible. Watch the switch from a relative word (fell by half) to an absolute one (low). It's like saying a 2,000-calorie dessert is healthy because you cut it in half. The argument needs the starting rate to have been low enough that half of it counts as low. Prephrase: the old rate wasn't so high that half is still high.

choices.note: Tempting, since it ties the drop to the rules. But too strong: 'not due to ANY other factor.' Negated, some other factor helped too, and the rules can still deserve credit. The argument survives.
choices.negation: The decline in the rate of lung disease among the district's miners was due at least partly to some factor other than the dust rules.

choices.note: Not required. Comparing with other districts doesn't tell us whether Ostrava's rate is low; all of them could be high or all low. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Miners in districts without similar rules do not develop lung disease at a higher rate than the district's miners now do.

choices.note: Way too strong. Low risk is compatible with some compliant miners getting sick. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one miner in the district who has fully complied with the dust rules over the past ten years has developed lung disease.

choices.note: Too strong. Other causes (like smoking) can exist and the risk can still be low. Negating doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Dust is not the only cause of lung disease among the miners who work underground in the Ostrava district.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the old rate was so high that half of it is still high. Then 'only a low risk' is false, and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: The district's former rate of lung disease was so high that even half that rate would still be high.

questions.stimulus: Many of the region's folktales are now known only to a few elderly storytellers. Recording these storytellers on audio is one of the most effective ways to help preserve the tales they tell. Therefore, if the region's folktales are to be preserved at all, the regional folklore society must fund an audio-recording program this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Only seeds stored in a cold vault remain viable for more than a few decades. Therefore, if the seed collection is to remain viable for that long, it must be stored in a cold vault.
Every heirloom apple variety that has survived to the present day was grafted by orchard keepers at some point. Therefore, any apple variety that orchard keepers graft will survive into the future.
Since watering in the evening is among the most effective ways to help tomato plants withstand heat, no tomato plant that goes without evening watering will withstand this summer's heat.
Some of the region's tomato growers use drip irrigation, and their plants withstood last summer's heat well. Therefore, all of the region's tomato growers should switch to drip irrigation this year.

Most of the professional gardeners surveyed by a gardening magazine recommend watering plants early in the morning. Therefore, a gardener who wants healthy plants should water them early in the morning.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from 'recording is one of the most effective ways to help' to 'recording is required.' (C) makes the same move, from one of the most effective ways to help tomatoes withstand heat to a necessary condition, but states its conclusion in contrapositive form ('no plant that goes without'). Most students pick (A), because it has the same 'if X is to happen, it must' conclusion; but (A)'s premise already says only cold-vault storage works, so its conclusion follows validly.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the folktales are to be preserved, the folklore society must fund an audio-recording program this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many tales are known only to a few elderly storytellers; recording them is one of the most effective ways to help preserve the tales.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X is one of the best ways to achieve Y; so if Y is to happen, X is required.

breakdown.analysis: 'One of the most effective ways' means there are others. Writing the tales down, video, training younger storytellers: any could work. So recording isn't required. The argument turns 'a great option' into 'the only option.' That's a scope shift from helpful to necessary. It's like saying running is one of the best ways to get fit, so anyone who doesn't run will never get fit. Prephrase: one of the best ways → must. The right answer hides it in contrapositive form: 'no plant that goes without X will Y' is the same as 'Y requires X.' Most students pick (A), because its conclusion has the same 'must' shape. But (A)'s premise says 'only,' so it's valid.

choices.note: Tempting, because its conclusion has the same 'if this is to happen, it must' shape. But its premise says ONLY cold-vault seeds stay viable. With 'only' in the premise, 'must' follows. Valid, so it can't match a flawed argument.
Reverses a conditional: surviving varieties were grafted, so grafted varieties will survive. A different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every champion swimmer trained daily, so anyone who trains daily will be a champion.

choices.note: CORRECT. Evening watering is 'among the most effective ways' to help, and the conclusion makes it required: no plant without it will withstand the heat. Same jump from one good way to a necessary condition, just in contrapositive form.
A hasty generalization from some growers to all, plus a recommendation. Not a helpful-to-required shift.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Two of my friends liked this phone, so everyone should buy it.

choices.note: An appeal to what most experts recommend. The conclusion is a recommendation, not a claim that morning watering is required.

questions.stimulus: Pet behaviorist: In a recent trial, owners of cats that habitually scratched furniture plugged a pheromone diffuser into an outlet in their homes. Over the following two weeks, furniture scratching in these households fell by about half compared with the two weeks before. So the diffuser offers cat owners a lasting solution to destructive scratching.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the pet behaviorist's argument?
choices: The pheromone released by the diffuser closely resembles one that cats themselves deposit when they rub their faces against objects.
Operating a pheromone diffuser continuously for a year costs more than buying several sturdy scratching posts.
Owners in the trial reported that their cats seemed noticeably calmer during the weeks the diffuser was in use.
Cats typically stop reacting to a newly introduced scent within a few weeks of first encountering it.
Scratching is a natural behavior that helps cats keep their claws in good condition and mark their territory.
questions.explanation: Two weeks of results are used to support a 'lasting' solution. (D) gives a reason to expect the effect to fade: the diffuser's scent was new to the cats, and cats soon stop reacting to new scents. Most students pick (C), because calmer cats seem relevant to the diffuser's effect; but it is irrelevant corroboration: it supports the short-term result the behaviorist already reported and says nothing about whether the effect lasts.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The diffuser offers a lasting solution to destructive scratching.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a trial, scratching fell by about half in the two weeks after owners plugged in the diffuser.

breakdown.analysis: Two weeks, and the conclusion says 'lasting'? That's the gap: a short-term result stretched into a long-term claim. To weaken, give a reason the effect would fade. The right answer doesn't say 'the effect fades.' It gives a general fact about cats: they stop reacting to new scents within weeks. Connect it to the trial: the diffuser's scent was new, so the drop may be a novelty effect. It's like judging a new alarm clock after its first week, before you learn to sleep through it. Most students pick (C), because calmer cats sound like evidence about the diffuser. But that only confirms the two-week result the behaviorist already has.

choices.note: Explains how the diffuser might work. That supports the short-term effect; it doesn't weaken anything.
Cost is a different dimension. A costly solution can still be lasting.
Tempting, because calm cats seem related to less scratching. But it only backs up the two-week result already reported. It says nothing about whether the effect lasts.
CORRECT. The diffuser's scent was new to the cats. If cats stop reacting to new scents within a few weeks, the drop in scratching is likely to fade, which undercuts 'lasting.'
Why cats scratch doesn't bear on whether the diffuser's effect lasts. Interesting fact, not relevant.

questions.stimulus: Transportation official: Critics claim that raising the speed limit on the Calloway Expressway from 90 to 110 kilometers per hour has made the expressway more dangerous. Yet in the two years since the change, the number of collisions per million vehicle-kilometers traveled on the expressway has actually declined slightly. So the critics are mistaken: the higher limit has not made the expressway any more dangerous.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the transportation official's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses the rate at which collisions occur on the expressway with the total number of collisions that occur there
treats evidence about how often a kind of event occurs as conclusive about how much danger it poses
presumes, without providing justification, that raising the speed limit caused the slight decline in the collision rate
rejects the critics' claim solely on the grounds that the critics have not proven that it is true
fails to consider that many drivers on the expressway may not obey the new, higher speed limit
questions.explanation: The official's evidence concerns how often collisions happen, but 'more dangerous' also covers how severe they are, and crashes at 110 km/h tend to cause worse injuries. (B) names the move from frequency to overall danger in abstract terms. Most students pick (A), because rate-versus-number is a familiar flaw and the stimulus gives a rate; but the official deliberately uses a rate rather than a raw count, which is the appropriate measure, so nothing is confused.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The higher limit has not made the expressway any more dangerous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Critics say it has; but collisions per million vehicle-km have declined slightly in the two years since the change.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer collisions per kilometer. Fine. But is collision frequency the whole story of danger? A crash at 110 km/h is far worse than one at 90. You could have slightly fewer crashes and many more deaths. The official measures how OFTEN, then concludes about how DANGEROUS. That's a measure mismatch, a kind of scope shift. It's like saying a sport isn't dangerous because injuries are rare, when every injury is a broken neck. We need an answer that says frequency was treated as the whole of danger. Most students pick (A), because they see a rate and reach for rate-versus-number. But using a rate here is correct. The problem is that frequency isn't the whole of danger.

choices.note: Tempting, because traffic volume might have changed. But the official uses a rate (per million vehicle-km), which is the right way to handle volume. Using a rate isn't confusing it with a total.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions rose from 50 to 60, so the road's collision rate must have gone up, even though traffic doubled.

choices.note: CORRECT. Collisions per kilometer measures how often crashes happen, not how bad they are. Higher speeds can make each crash deadlier, so 'not more dangerous' doesn't follow.
The official only says danger didn't increase. That needs no claim that the higher limit CAUSED the decline.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions fell after the limit rose, so raising the limit made the road safer.

choices.note: Tempting if you skim: it sounds like a rebuttal. But the official offers actual evidence (the collision rate), not just the critics' lack of proof.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Critics haven't proven the limit is dangerous, so it's safe.

choices.note: So? The conclusion is about what happened after the limit changed, whatever drivers actually did. Disobedience doesn't make the reasoning flawed.
